Question: What is a traditional Southern-style cornmeal-based "hush puppy," and where does it get its name from (i.e., what was once commonly used to feed dogs)?
Answer: Hush Puppies are delightful to eat, easy to make and are fun to toss to begging dogs (“Hush, puppy), the most logical reason for the name. If you are going fishing and plan on making a shore dinner, then make the batter up in advance, put it into a container, keep it cold and then cook your hush puppies before you cook your fish: Gives you and the pups an appetizer. INGREDIENTS 1 1/2 cups fine- or medium-grind cornmeal 1/2 cup all-purpose flour 1 1/2 teaspoons kosher salt 1 1/2 teaspoons baking powder 1/2 teaspoon baking soda 1/2 teaspoon granulated sugar (optional) 1/2 small yellow onion 1 large egg 1 cup buttermilk 4 cups peanut or vegetable oil, for deep frying TIPS: Cornmeal: If you are using self-rising cornmeal and flour omit the baking powder and salt for the recipe. This will ensure a lighter batter. Add-ins: Add in minced jalapeños or red pepper flakes for a little more heat. Switch out your favorite seasonings to make different variations. Batter Tip: It is best not to over mix the batter. If the batter looks lumpy that is okay. Dropping batter into oil: For an easier way to drop the balls into the batter I like to use a cookie dough scooper to not only for the round balls but also drop them in without using my fingers. It is a cleaner and easier way. Cooking spray: To make it easier when dropping the batter into the oil, simply spray cooking spray on the cookie dough scooper or your spoon that you are using to help relieve the sticky batter into the oil. Oil: I used a peanut oil for taste but it also does the best at high temperatures when deep frying. Vegetable oil or canola oil work well too. Olive oil is not a deep frying oil to use. To test the oil to make sure it is hot enough, drop in one inch batter and see how quickly it fries. It should be 2 to 3 minutes of frying spinning it around. Once the mixture is mixed together evenly continue to add in more hush puppies batter to the hot oil cooking these quickly. Serve with a side of tarter sauce and enjoy! Keep warm: While making several hush puppies, place the hush puppies in an oven safe pan and let them rest in the oven at the lowest temperature (about 200 degrees Fahrenheit). Do not over bake your hush puppies though. The maximum amount of time in the oven is about 15 to 20 minutes.

Question: How can we train our family’s Golden Doodle to not bite when food she's stolen off a table is taken away? She guards it, becomes very aggressive and bites. No amount of firm talking or threatening works.
Answer: The first step is for you to decide that your role is that of a “puppy parent” — not that of a playmate. She must believe in you and care enough to do what you say — certainly while you are right there with her — and know what you expect her to do and how she is to do it. Your dog must trust you so much that she will do something contrary to her animal nature because you told her to. She must know that when you tell her to “drop it” — her response must be an immediate “drop.” She must also understand that “drop” is a serious command that she knows how to fulfill. She must believe that you will reward her (Good girl!) with praise and affection because you are proud of her because she has fulfilled your trust. She must also understand that misbehavior has immediate consequences, from a strong “NO!” to (in our case with our 180-pound English mastiff) being subjected to a “time out” that enforces our intolerance of unacceptable behavior. Biting cannot ever be tolerated. Teach her the “drop” command by showing her — with one of her toys — and praise and petting. Make sure she understands. Always reward her with love and attention. Be firm and consistent. After you are certain she understands, then tell her to “drop” the stolen food. Consistent, gentle training will earn her respect and trust: It becomes a constant in her life. You owe it to her to teach her how to behave, how to fit into her family and into society.

Question: Is it scary for dogs to fly in cargo?
Answer: As a person who honors the mutual commitment made between my dog and me, I would never, ever consider flying my dog in cargo. My dog deserves better. I deserve better. Risking damage to my dog’s life, health and psyche is totally unacceptable. Putting a dog in cargo, to be unprotected from the heat/cold, the darkness, the frightening sounds and the fearsome smells and the possibility of depressurization (making it impossible to breathe) is madness. I would be terrified of flying cargo. Wouldn’t you? My dog belongs to me: I take careful care of what is mine. If I can not take my dog safely with me, then I have always chosen either to pay someone to stay with my dog in our home or I have skipped the trip. I know because I have faced this quandary. When my husband of 37 years died unexpectedly and very quickly of pancreatic cancer at age 60, I was left alone with no family except our dog Lady — a mongrel dog found wandering, terrified and near-death in a Louisiana RV park post-Katrina — whom we had adopted and taken with us in our traveling. Lady became an integral part of our family and went everywhere with us. When we went off in our Jeep, she went too. We hiked together, slept together, did nearly everything as a three-some. Because Lady had been so hurt and damaged, she was very fearful of being left alone, without us. So, it took months before she could believe that , although we might leave her in our RV or in our Jeep, we would always come back to her. She was safe with us. Lady was a willing, devoted companion — both to my husband (the light of her life) and to me. She helped us feel safe, too. When he was dying, she helped comfort him and shared this total devotion with me. In making a new life for myself so that I could go on, I strongly considered moving to the UK, so I went to work on how to get us safely over the Atlantic to a dog-welcoming country and then on into England. Flying her cargo was not a consideration once I investigated what might happen to her. No. Way too risky and totally off-putting. From Louisiana, I considered driving us north to Canada, then taking a ferry and shipping and chartered flights — to cross over the North Atlantic — hop-skipping our way across via Greenland, Iceland, etc., to Ireland/Scotland. Creative, but impractical. So, I concluded that flying her (a large, German-shepherd-looking dog) cargo was the only likely way for us to travel. Consequently, going to England with Lady was a non-starter. Bottom line: I went to England (Two weeks: Brighton and London, including the Chelsea Flower Show), while Lady stayed home in our rental house, fed and walked and cared for by a mutual friend. I compromised my desires because Lady was more important to me that moving to England. What you choose to do is up to you. But I strongly suggest that you face the facts — as I did — and do what you know is right for you. and for your dog.

Question: Which dog is better as a family dog, a Labrador Retriever or a Beagle?
Answer: Without exception, I would choose the Labrador retriever. Labrador retrievers are “family dogs” — they are happy, happy retrieving toys and tennis balls and playing with your kids. These dogs love the water, love their family and want to be included in everything you do. We didn’t have children, so our neighbor’s kids used to come over to play “hide and seek” with our Lab. Yep, they’d hide her ball in our house (started out with the ball being put behind a living room chair) while one of the kids distracted Cracker (our dog). Any hiding spot was “fair” as long as Cracker could successfully find the ball and retrieve it easily. This was great fun for all of them. My husband took Cracker dove hunting (baited field, no walking through snake-infested brush and such, “hunt” for an hour or so, then quit and have in-field cocktails and such), but only during “dove season”. Labs are happy, easy-going dogs who want to please their families. They love life and having a good time. Labs are gentle, easily trainable dogs —- who need everyone in the family to work the same way with the puppy, use the same words, train gently and kindly, and be consistent. Labs love everyone, so they will bark, but are not to be trained as “attack dogs” — their nature is to welcome folks, wag and bring a ball (Want to play fetch?). Beagles are wonderful dogs but they like to howl and should never be off lead when they are not behind a fence: Beagles are known for deciding it’s time to hunt and darting off after the prey, baying and howling as they go. Oops! So, yep the Lab is a winner!

Question: Put a deposit down for a Golden Retriever puppy over a year ago wanting a male. The breeder claims she has not had any males and she's had litters consistently. Does this seem fishy?
Answer: Yes, this sounds as if the breeder is a crook. Get your deposit returned ASAP. Remember, you have the legal power, not the breeder. Step 1: If you do not have an email or a text-response — legal evidence in court — from this breeder that says “no males” and the amount of your deposit, then get one: Set the breeder up with an email/text that you have written — stating what you have been promised, how much you have paid and demanding your deposit be returned immediately. This should prompt a reply from the breeder. Keep the breeder’s reply: The breeder’s answer is legal evidence. Step 2: If the breeder does not return your deposit, then send an email/text — followed up with a certified letter — notifying the breeder that the breeder is forcing you to take legal action. Include these three in this second communication with the breeder: 1 You have evidence of the breeder’s contract (breeder’s email/text reply and, likely, the puppy contract itself). 2 The AKC (or whatever) has the records of all the pups born since you gave the breeder your deposit and has on file whether a male has been born. (This is a matter of public record, available to be subpoenaed by the court.) 3 Set a specific deadline — within a week or so — for you to have in hand either cash or a cashier’s check from the breeder for the full amount. Then sit back and wait to see what happens. If you have to, you have the evidence you need to take the breeder to court. You can represent yourself (no lawyer) in Small Claims Court, unless the deposit is too much for this court. If it’s too much, then a letter from an attorney should spur immediate action from the breeder. Whatever damages you can think of might also come into play: Not only have you been ripped off, but also you have suffered the deprivation of being able to buy your puppy — which you had needed for companionship and comfort during this global pandemic, etc. While you are getting your money back, have fun! You have the power, not the breeder. So, go for it!

Question: Why do Great Pyrenees have extra toes?
Answer: “Great Pyrenees are famous for their double dew claws. Most dogs have a dewclaw; what seems to an "extra" toe on their limbs that is more proximal to the body. Some owners have these removed often during spay/neuter. The theory is that they are vestigial appendages and can cause damage if they are left on the dog. The dog may snag or tear them during their normal play or work. “For Great Pyrenees, these appendages are a breed standard. They are often a breed disqualifier in show circuits if they do not have them. Functionally, the extra "two toes" are there to offer more leverage and grip while they are navigating their terrain performing their livestock duties. As non-livestock friends, we keep them because they are a breed trait and often owners find no drawback to retaining them. “Some dewclaws (and double dewclaws) are more "floppy" than others. Some dogs with these appendages can use them quite effectively to add extra grip to their step. Other dogs, they seem more non-functional and seem to hang. Either way, they are not "dead" appendages, and have an adequate amount of blood supply and tendons nonetheless.”

Lightening your yards with outdoor lights or motion-sensor lights will help discourage coyotes from prowling there. Tip 7. Create an Unwelcome Environment for Coyotes Coyotes can easily hop over 6 feet fences to sneak in your yards for food. To protect dogs from coyotes, you shall set up 7+ feet high coyote-proof fences with coyote spikes, PVC pipes or chicken wire that push off any climbing coyotes. Once the coyotes treat your neighborhood as their source of food and shelters, they will become bolder and chase after your pet dogs and even small children and adults if they are not well fed. Meanwhile, you may feed the coyotes without being aware of it by feeding your pet dogs outside your home. Remember to leave no pet food and eliminate the water sources in the yards. It doesn’t mean that the coyotes have given up upon your pet dogs and you. The best thing to protect your dogs from coyotes is to keep hazing them with the three methods above until they run out of your sight. Tip 5. Don’t Turn Your Back to Them or Try to Run A piece of research on coyote attacks has indicated that hazing is the most effective method to protect pet dogs from coyotes while the least feasible way is to turn your back to that wild animals and run. If you do so, you are exposing your backs to the coyotes and they will chase after you in no time by their nature. You believe that you can run faster than the coyotes? Trust me, these wild creatures can surpass and attack you within minutes. The safest way is to step back slowly while hazing them at the same time. Tip 6. Don’t Use Poison or Kill Coyotes without Licenses Trapping or killing the coyotes on your own can never be your first option to protect dogs from coyotes. Without sufficient hunting experience, you may get attacked by the coyotes if the killing fails. Even veteran hunters need to acquire licenses from local authorities before hunting coyotes. Moreover, using poison to kill coyotes may lead to bad consequences. For example, other predators in the wild will get poisoned and infected as well if they have eaten dead coyotes that carry fatal parasites and diseases. Tip 7. Report to Animal Control or Other Local Authorities Local authorities know the best how to deal with coyote issues. So when you are safe after confronting or spotting coyotes in your neighborhood, contact the professionals and report to them as soon as possible. It is beneficial to protect dogs from coyotes in your neighborhood and bring coyote issues to the forefront as well. With your reports, local and national researchers will understand the coyote problems better and thus, they will be able to offer more possible solutions to avoid the conflicts between coyotes and humans.”

Question: Is the English Mastiff extinct?
Answer: No, the English mastiff is not extinct. Not yet. Yours is a reasonable question, though, because the English mastiff would have been extinct following WWII except for a few breeders who either hid their dogs or sent them to Canada. Canada has been vitally important for saving the English mastiff because of providing a safe place for breeding stock. Without Canada, the English mastiff likely would no longer exist. After WWII, rebuilding the English mastiff in England itself was not easy because England and the world had been ripped apart. FYI: WWII was a global disaster, with major effects on the entire world, the European continent devastated and broken by war, and the UK (England, etc.) being the last bastion holding out against Hitler’s Germany, etc. Had the U.S. not entered the war, Hitler (et al) would have won. The UK was being bombed into oblivion. Everything and everyone in the UK was at risk. No one had enough food. Ration coupons were issued for flour, cloth, gas, etc. Things were really, really bad. There was not enough food to feed people, so “pets” were an unnecessary luxury. Many, many pets were killed, including English mastiffs. Not to do so would have been “unpatriotic”. “As many as 750,000 British pets were killed:” The English mastiff is a dog that mostly the “landed gentry” owned and valued, so some owners had the wherewithal and the connections to smuggle dogs out of the country and sent them to Canada for the duration of the war. But the war took a long time. English mastiffs are short-lived. Trying to preserve a varied bloodline proved very, very difficult. Consequently, the English mastiff — a war dog that accompanied Julius Caesar on his military campaigns — ironically was nearly completely destroyed by war. Somehow, barely, the breed has survived — until now. In the United States, the English mastiff bloodline is again under attack. This time by breeders and the AKC because big, heavy, cumbersome “bubbas” are now popular. English mastiffs are being systematically destroyed by fools who put their own hubris and egos over the well-being of the dogs. Today’s AKC English mastiffs are very, very likely to be too big for their bone structure. So, if you are considering looking for a real English mastiff, do not settle for half-breeds like the American mastiff. Do not settle for big, “bubba” dogs. Use the internet to look at and find a breeder producing English mastiffs that look like ours. (These are ours: Trixie, 150 pounds, 8 years old and her little “brother”, a 6-months-old puppy, who will weigh about 180 when grown.) Then go to see and meet this puppy/dog. You must both want one another. You both will know. English mastiffs are a two-way street. A true English mastiff is an inside, sleep-on-your-bed dog that wants to be with you at all times and will stand by you and protect you through anything that comes. These are gentle, big-hearted dogs who shed and drool and sling that drool. They are lazy lie-abouts, who are happy just to watch over their people and want only to be petted and loved. They will love and protect their own. Generally, their size is so off-putting that folks will not “push it” with you or your dog. An English mastiff person must be willing to be a “parent”: These are strong-willed dogs who will overrule their master if the dog knows this is necessary (if the dog senses a stroke coming on, etc.). It is imperative to have a loving, gentle relationship with an English mastiff because he/she deserves nothing less. Best wishes for your and yours to be safe, healthy and happy, Leslie

Question: How do you make an oatmeal shampoo for dogs?
Answer: “Homemade Oatmeal Dog Shampoo From the American Kennel Club: “Oatmeal Dog Shampoo for Dry Skin Ingredients: Grind the oatmeal in a coffee grinder or food processor until it’s the consistency of flour. Pour into a large bowl and mix in baking soda. Add warm water and stir until incorporated. Wet your dog with warm water and then lather him up with your homemade shampoo. Work into his coat and allow it to sit for a few minutes, if he’ll let you. Then rinse thoroughly and dry.” “One thing you don’t want to use is shampoo made for humans. The pH level of our skin is different from that of dogs: ours ranges from 5.5-5.6, while dogs’ pH is between 6.2-7.4. Human shampoo will be too acidic for dogs and can cause skin irritations. “If you’re going to mix up your own dog shampoo, you’ll be aiming for a pH level around 7. Luckily, others have done the math for you and devised simple homemade dog shampoo recipes. Basic Homemade Dog Shampoo 3-Ingredient Simple Shampoo Dish detergent is formulated to cut through grease and will do a great job of washing away oils that accumulate on your dog’s coat and skin. White vinegar has antibacterial and deodorant properties and will leave his coat shiny and clean. Just be careful not to get any in his eyes. Ingredients: Combine all ingredients in a spray bottle and shake to mix. Then wet your dog’s coat with warm water and spray with shampoo, avoiding his eyes. Work the shampoo into his coat, creating a thick lather. Rinse thoroughly and repeatedly, even if you think all signs of shampoo are gone. Then dry him off, and he’s good to go!” Wishing you and yours stay safe, healthy and happy, Leslie

Question: How much should a pitbull puppy eat per day? How do you decide?
Answer: Feed your puppy “puppy food”. Puppy food has the nutrients your pup needs for strong, controlled growth. Set up a regular schedule and make sure to feed your puppy — puppy-size portions — at least four times a day. Plan to take your puppy to pee/poop before you feed and after he/she eats. You will need to protect your pup against “accidents” in the house: Remember a little puppy’s body is still forming — so pups cannot control their sphincter muscles. Your pup will need your help to be successful. So, take him/her to the area you have designated for this purpose every time you play with your pup, when the pup wakes up, when the pup has done pretty much anything that can make his/her little body need relief. “Since puppies grow quickly, they need to eat highly nutritious food and they need it often. Since they tend to burn so much energy, you'll start out feeding your puppy frequently, then slowly wean them down to less regular feedings. This process will help them grow big and strong. “6 to 12 Weeks: Puppies should be eating food nutritionally designed to meet their needs for bone and muscle growth…A quality puppy food contains optimal amounts of protein, DHA, and vitamins to keep your puppy growing at appropriate rates. For puppies, four feedings a day are recommended for ages six to twelve weeks. It's also a good idea to start puppies with moistened food to help them chew. “3 to 6 Months: Feedings can decrease to three times a day during this period. You will see your puppy start to mature during this phase — their baby potbelly and pudginess will start to disappear. Its recommended to feed them puppy-sized portions until you see signs that their body is maturing. “6 to 12 Months: At this age, reduce to twice-daily feedings. Keep in mind that after your dog is neutered, their energy level may decrease, so it may be a good time to switch from nutrient-rich puppy food to adult food. While you should always check with your vet about your puppies specific growth, typically smaller breeds should transition to adult food at 10-12 months, while larger breeds may take a little longer — 12–14 months or even longer. Bigger breeds should continue on puppy food longer, up to 14 months.” We fed both our English mastiffs (150+ pounds as adults) “puppy food” for over a year and a half. Wishing you and yours stay safe, healthy and happy, Leslie

Question: What is the best age to neuter a male Siberian Husky?
Answer: Tricky, isn’t it? We have an English mastiff (now about 180+ pounds) so it became a balancing act: Let him mature enough for the “growth plates” (at each end of every long bone) to develop fully so that he will have the strong bones his big body will need to support itself. Neutering too soon messes this up. Your vet can explain and help you and your dog. But, on the other hand, our vet advised not waiting too long because the “male hormones” will likely cause changes in his personality — make him “manly” and hot to trot. Generally, we were told, this is not reversible. Well, oops! We put our vet in charge. We neutered Shomer at about a year and a half. I am not sure if this was the right timing to do this. He seems OK, but we’ve never had him x-rayed to check his bones and how their “growth plates” developed. We are careful with him because English mastiffs must be protected so that they do not jump around and play too hard, which can damage their bodies. Also English mastiffs — like all big dogs (probably including a Siberian Husky) can get torsion (twists in their intestines) which can kill the dog painfully. So, only time will tell about the effects on his physical body. English mastiffs live, in general, 6 to 12 years. My dog Trixie lived a great life until she was 8. Shomer is 4, so who knows? One thing that is certain is that Shomer — with his family — is the most gentle male dog we have ever met. He is cuddly and loving and wants to snuggle up, be hugged and petted. Is this because we neutered him too soon? Or is it because we are all so very lucky, lucky? Wishing you and yours stay safe, healthy and happy, Leslie

Question: Are Rhodesian Ridgebacks calm?
Answer: You have asked if a Rhodesian Ridgeback is calm (and earlier, you asked about loyal). I do not know personally about a Rhodesian Ridgeback, but I do know a whole big lot about English mastiffs. These dogs are similar in many ways. I looked up info about the Rhodesian Ridgeback and will compare this to what I know by experience about English mastiffs. I think this might help you. First, both the Rhodesian Ridgeback (RR from now on) and the English mastiff (EM) are big, strong dogs that are able to think for themselves and act on their own to handle issues. RRs weigh less than 100 pounds, so they are not as big as an EM (Our male dog “Shomer” weighs 180+ pounds). Both these dogs are very strong. EMs like to guard their families by putting themselves in between any possible threat to their family. When working as our service dog, Shomer is always on alert. EMs prefer to be laid back and lazy, preferring to sit or lie down and be comfortable and relaxed. EMs require minimal exercise, preferably walking with the family. If you throw a ball for an EM, the dog may choose to bring it back to you once or twice or so, but after that you are on your own: You want it? You go get it yourself — I’ve done my bit. RRs, on the other hand, “How much exercise does a Rhodesian Ridgeback need? two hours exercise Your Ridgeback will need a minimum of two hours exercise every day. This needs to be several long walks with plenty of off-lead exercise in a secure place. On top of this, you'll also need to do lots with your Rhodesian Ridgeback to keep their brain active.” For me, a LOL (little old lady), this makes a RR a non-starter because I cannot do these things: My dog deserves better than this from me. Both EMs and RRs are serious, big dogs with independent spirits. An EM needs to be willing to overrule his/her master because the EM trusts his own judgement about protecting: This means that an EM will make his master sit down and be quiet if the dog senses (via smell or sound) that the master is in going to be in physical difficulty (stroke, heart attack). All dogs can sense these things — the master just needs to pay attention to the dog and learn to read the dog’s signals. RRs are also independent: “Rhodesian Ridgebacks are highly intelligent and learn quickly making them ideal candidates for training. However, they are also stubborn, independent, and very much have a mind of their own. This means they can be difficult to train and need very strong guidance and ownership.” Jan 19, 2019 So, bottom line, what do you think now? For myself, I know that a RR and I would not make a good pairing. I partner for life and love my dogs. Consequently, I do my best to identify what kind of dog I want and then look for someone who has earned my trust to help me find my new dog. My suggestion to you (if you have not already done so) is to make a list of what you want in your dog. I’d start with calm and loyal. Then I’d think about how much activity I wanted to do with my dog and choose a breed that wants and needs the same things I do. Example: If I do not want to “throw the ball, throw the ball”, then I should not choose a Labrador retriever. I’ve thought about this myself and am beginning to think about poodles. They come in three sizes and various colors. They’re smart, trainable, have been around a long time and seem to fit well with LOLs. For me, having my dog cut up in some fancy manner is not my style, so I think I’d take scissors and trim my dog up myself: Keep the hair short and comfortable for both of us. But, who’s to say? Honestly, it’s likely that I will go down to our local animal shelters to meet and talk with the folks who work there. I’m afraid that if I go in to look at the dogs, I will want to take them all home, so I can’t handle this. My idea — when I am ready to have another dog — is to interact with the folks at the shelter. They’ll be able to look at me and draw their own conclusions as I tell them what I want in my dog and what I have to give. If they have a dog that they think will suit me, then I’ll ask them to put me and the dog together. If the dog likes me and I like the dog, then that’s it. The bonding has to be mutual: I will never accept a dog that someone else — like a breeder, for example — picks out for me and tells me that this is the one I get. Oh, no. Never. My dogs are chosen by me. We have personal contact. We interact. We show each other that this is what we want. We form an immediate bond that will grow stronger over time. I wish you well in your search for your dog. Wishing you and yours stay safe, healthy and happy, Leslie

Question: Do martingale collars help with pulling?
Answer: Like anything else, a martingale collar’s effectiveness depends on how it is being used. If it is used properly — with a quick snap of the wrist (to apply reasonable pressure with the collar to the dog’s throat) and released immediately — then yes the collar works. If the dog is allowed to pull against the collar, that is a big oops. If the walker chooses to pull/drag the dog using the collar, that too is a big oops. Suggestion: Pretend you are the dog’s “parent”. Be in control and show this. I suggest first sitting the dog (Sit command and at the same time using the collar to pull up and back on the dog, while pushing down with your hand atop his/her rear), then say either “heel” if you are going to formally walk your dog or “walk” if you are going to let your dog wander at will while on lead. (Be certain that your dog knows what you want and is trained to know how and what to do.) Finally — after you’ve said “heel” or “walk” step forward and begin. (If the dog does not understand, then stop. Sit the dog again. Show him/her again.) I suggest you train your dog to stop when you stop. To sit at your “sit” command. To lie down (“down”) at your command. Whether you are a pair out to see the sights or you are guiding your dog in a public place, where you need your dog under your control, your dog deserves to be trained properly by you so that you two can be comfortable together. Wishing you and yours stay safe, healthy and happy, Leslie

Question: How do you choose a name for your golden retriever?
Answer: When I choose a name for my dog, I decide what I want to think about my dog and what I want other people to think. One’s name has meaning and evokes emotion. Sometimes emotion doesn’t matter. For example, as a girl I named my cocker spaniel “Ginger”. Yep, she had “ginger-colored” hair and was full of life and spunky. Her name made us both happy, happy because it fit her looks and her personality. To me, “Ginger” was perfect. Sometimes the name needs to matter with other people. My husband and I adopted a mixed breed stray that was starving, needy, and pitiful. She saw my husband walking in a RV park, followed him, and came to him when he got down and asked. They walked together: His hand gently held in her mouth. The “oops” with her was that she was big, mostly German Shepherd, untrained and had been so abused that she feared most everything and everyone, including cigarettes (Had she been burned?) and fishing poles (beaten?). She was bedraggled, frightened and frightening. So, we made up a story (Hurricane Katrina survivor-rescue) and a name that would evoke positive thoughts: We called her “Lady.” Yep, worked like a charm because everyone seems to like a gal who is a lady and, with the background story, people wanted to help her get through her pain. “Lady” was perfect. Other times it matters to the one with the dog. My husband named his English mastiff (adult size 180+ pounds) “Shomer”. “Shomer” is the command that God gave Adam and Eve about the garden: Guard and protect. Our “Shomer” is a service dog, who is our intimate companion, our family member, and who “guards and protects” us, which is what “Shomer” means in Hebrew. Just saying our dog’s name helps us feel more secure. For us, “Shomer” is perfect. So, when you name your dog, why not think about the effect the name will have on both you and your dog? Have fun! Be creative! Choose the name that for you and your dog will be perfect. Wishing you and yours stay safe, healthy and happy, Leslie

Question: Are half-choke collars cruel?
Answer: If this is what you mean (first photo below) by a half-choke collar, then I think it could be useful in training — especially if your trainer demands you use a choke collar. Others I have looked at are frightening to me because the collar does not seem to quickly release. Think about it: The control here is to choke the dog. Choking risks injury to the dog — especially the dog’s throat, with a possibility of serious damage. A choke collar is used with a very quick, loose snap of the wrist and an instantaneous release. Having a wider, webbed “throat choke” would seem to help prevent damage to the dog’s throat. In training our English mastiffs (will weigh 150+ pounds as adults), we use this pinch collar, which exerts control with round-tipped spikes. Both collars are for TRAINING. As with any choke collar, a dog wearing one and left alone can get the collar caught up on something: The dog is left to choke to death and die. Our dogs are service dogs so they are always with us, all the time. When we go out in public, our dogs wear these collars — to make strangers feel safer because we can reach down and hold our dog’s collar as the dog sits and waits. (Our dogs are perfectly trained by us, so we know we can rely on the dog — people are a different matter because most folks simply do not understand polite behavior.) The cruelty issue, it seems to me, is whether or not the human using a collar on a dog is competent and kind. Wishing you and yours stay safe, healthy and happy, Leslie

Question: What breed of dog you recommend for family, children and partly with guarding characters among these Siberian Husky, Labrador or Golden Retriever?
Answer: You are considering three outstanding dog breeds with different characteristics because they have been bred to do different things. A Siberian Husky is a working dog — big and strong enough to pull a sled, of sturdy physique to last a long time and of a mind that makes the dog unwilling to give up. Difficult to train, demanding strong control and physical activity, this breed is not one I could ever recommend for you and your family. Labradors and Golden Retrievers are sporting dogs that like to be with people and are bred to “retrieve” things: A duck hunter’s bird from the water, a quail or duck in the field or a tennis ball tossed by a kid. Both of these breeds are well-suited to be family dogs. Either one would be a great choice for you. Think about what you want to do with your dog and how you want to live. If you live on the water or have a swimming pool, you need to know that Labradors love the water. Labs love to fetch and fetch and fetch. Labs shed and generally do not need brushing and washing to keep them looking good — unless they find and roll in something “doggie wonderful” that you find repulsive. Labs are loving and loyal. They welcome everyone they know but can be counted on to bark a warning and to defend their families if necessary. Golden Retrievers are very much like Labradors, except that they generally are less driven to fetch balls and such, have longer silkier hair that does require brushing and combing (to prevent matting) and generally love to cuddle up close with their families. Goldens seem more “laid back” than Labradors. So, if you want a slower, “snugglier” relationship with your dog and family, then I think a Golden is a better choice — especially if combing/brushing your dog will bring you pleasure. If you want a “let’s go” and “let’s play fetch” relationship with a dog who loves you and wants to please and needs you to play with him, then you likely will prefer a Labrador Retriever. Because these dogs have floppy ears that cover the ear canal you need to be careful to keep checking their ears: Just look inside and sniff the ear. If it’s clean (no red, no black ick) and smells “doggie” not icky, then everything is OK. If not, then we use Zymox Otic Enzymatic Solution for Dogs and Cats to Soothe Ear Infections Without Hydrocortisone: Without cleaning the ear, gently squirt a bunch of this stuff into each ear (if one is messed up, the other is likely to be as well, so get it now) and let the little enzymes eat up the ick. The enzymes do a great job (put in every day for a week or so). If the problem persists, then there’s something big-time wrong (a nasty infection) that needs antibiotics from the vet. In 20+ years of using Zymox, the enzymes have done the job perfectly except for one time that the vet needed to prescribe a specific infection-killing medicine. Perfect! Both of these breeds are easy to train and deserve your dedication to teaching them what they need to know to be successful. Think of each pup as a child — that can’t hold its urine as a baby, so needs you to take him to his potty place every time he wakes up, before and after he plays, and at regular intervals throughout the day and night. Question: How do you make homemade hush puppies?
Answer: HERE’S A FIRST-CLASS RECIPE FOR REALLY GOOD HUSH PUPPIES: IF YOU’RE GOING FISHING AND WANT TO COOK YOUR “SHORE DINNER” OUTSIDE ON THE BEACH, DO WHAT THE FISHING GUIDES DO — MAKE UP YOUR HUSH PUPPY MIX IN ADVANCE, THEN PUT YOUR MIX IN WITH THE BEER AND DRINKS IN YOUR COOLER. BE SURE TO PACK A BIG ROLL OF PAPER TOWELS, COOKING OIL, A FRYING PAN AND A SLOTTED SPOON. THE TIME FOR HAVING FUN IS RIGHT NOW — SO GO FOR IT! YIELD: Serves 4 to 6, Makes 18 to 20 hush puppies PREP TIME: 5 minutes COOK TIME: 12 minutes to 16 minutes INGREDIENTS 1 1/2 cups fine- or medium-grind cornmeal 1/2 cup all-purpose flour 1 1/2 teaspoons kosher salt 1 1/2 teaspoons baking powder 1/2 teaspoon baking soda 1/2 teaspoon granulated sugar (optional) 1/2 small yellow onion 1 large egg 1 cup buttermilk 4 cups peanut or vegetable oil, for deep frying INSTRUCTIONS 1. Prepare plate for draining hush puppies: Line a large plate with a double layer of paper towels. 2. Combine the dry ingredients: Whisk 1 1/2 cups cornmeal, 1/2 cup all-purpose flour, 1 1/2 teaspoons kosher salt, 1 1/2 teaspoons baking powder, 1/2 teaspoon baking soda, and 1/2 teaspoon granulated sugar, if using, together in a large bowl. 3. Prepare the wet ingredients and add to the dry: Grate 1/2 small yellow onion on the large holes of a box grater (about 1/4 cup) and add to the bowl. Add 1 large egg and 1 cup buttermilk. 4. Mix and “rest” the batter: Stir until combined. Set aside for 15 minutes while the oil heats. 5. Heat the oil and prepare a plate for draining the hush puppies: Add enough peanut or vegetable oil to a Dutch oven for a depth of 1 1/2 inches (about 4 cups). Heat over medium-high heat to 365ºF. 6. Fry the hush puppies in batches: Use a small ice cream scoop to drop golf ball-sized rounds (about 2 tablespoons each) of the batter into the oil, about 5 at a time. Make sure not to crowd the pot which will cause the oil temperature to drop. Turn the hush puppies frequently with a slotted spoon or tongs until deeply browned on all sides, 3 to 4 minutes. 7. Drain the hush puppies and serve: Transfer with a slotted spoon to the paper towels to drain. Repeat with the remaining batter, adjusting the heat to maintain the oil temperature. Serve hot with salted butter. Storage: Hush puppies are best eaten immediately after cooking. Store at room temperature for up to 1 day. THE RECIPE ADVICE: For “homemade hush puppies, opt for a fine- to medium-grind cornmeal, and spring for stone-ground. Mass-market cornmeal can give the fritters an unappealingly gritty texture. As for color, anything goes — both white and yellow are great. (FRANKLY, I THINK THAT “GRITTY” HUSH PUPPIES, MADE WITH “MASS-MARKET CORNMEAL” ARE REALLY GOOD.) How to Serve Hush Puppies The best hush puppies are served hot enough to burn your fingertips. After the crispy browned balls of cornmeal are pulled from the bubbling oil, drain them on a paper towel-lined plate to remove any excess cooking grease. From there, pile them in a basket destined for the middle of the table or add a few to your plate. They’re the perfect accompaniment to Southern classics like fried fish and barbecue, but don’t stop there. Split the hush puppies open, add a pat of salted butter, and serve with anything you’ve got on the menu. WISHING YOU AND YOURS STAY SAFE, HEALTHY AND HAPPY, LESLIE

Question: What types of frogs are poisonous to dogs in Florida?
Answer: Invasive, non-Florida toads are poisonous. Native Florida toads are not. Native Florida toads secrete a substance on their backs that protects the toad and makes the dog salivate (froth at the mouth). It must be uncomfortable for the dog and being crushed is deadly for the toad, but some dogs never seem to care and keep biting frogs anyway. Obviously, Florida toads do not kill dogs. The Florida Wildlife Extension folks have a definitive answer: “The toxin from the Marine/Cane/Giant Toad -- scientific name Rhinella marina (formerly Bufo marinus) -- can be hazardous, sometimes fatal, to pets. In Florida, they are only found in the southeastern coastal region (Dade Co. and Monroe County), a small area on the southwest coast (Lee and Glades County), and a small area near Tampa (Pinellas County and nearby areas). So, Marine Toads will only be a threat if you live in or near those areas of Florida. Adult Marine Toads can be bigger than your fist, much larger than any toad or frog that is native to Florida. Remember that ALL toads have glands on their skin that contain MILD toxins that just taste nasty or make a potential predator a little sick after they try to eat a toad. The strategy for the toxin is to "educate" the predator to not mess with toads again. But the Marine Toad is NOT NATIVE to Florida and the animals here are not adapted to its toxin, that's why it is a more serious threat. The toxin of Marine Toads can make humans sick if swallowed, so be SURE to wash your hands immediately after touching a Marine Toad. Also, if you accidentally rub your eyes before washing hands, the toxin can irritate your eyes. If you see a toad that you suspect might be a Marine Toad, first, make SURE it is the Marine Toad (they can look similar to our native Southern toad, which is harmless to pets, they just taste bad). Look at photos and information at Frogs and Toads of Florida and compare the Southern Toad to the Marine Toad. Also refer to the publication, "Marine Toads (Bufo marinus)." All toads go through a growth stage, so all species at one time or another are small (so it is not safe to assume that all small toads are not Marine Toad species). For Marine Toads, they will not have as much toxin when they are small, but they can still be dangerous. Marine Toads have large, parotoid glands that angle downward onto the shoulders (by comparison, the Southern Toad has parotoid glands that are kidney-bean-shaped and small). Also, the Southern Toad has two ridges just inside the eyes that end in bulbous knobs. The Marine Toad does not have these ridges or knobs.”

Question: How do I manage excessive dog drool?
Answer: We have two 150-pound+ English mastiffs, so let’s talk drool: “Drool” is part of the breed: All English mastiffs drool. As puppies, they seem like other pups, but then as the pup develops into a dog, here comes the drool. Why? Look at the dog’s mouth: Extra-wide, which causes drooping lips on both sides. These drooping lips form pockets inside the dog’s mouth that allow saliva to build up. Too much saliva-build up bothers the dog, likely because it tickles. A shake of the head will sling off the drool. Dogs cannot wipe their mouths with a napkin, so what do do? The only way that I know of to keep doggie drool off the walls, etc., is to wipe the dog’s mouth — as you would with a little baby — immediately after the dog drinks, eats, runs, etc. Yep, unless you want to be a maid wiping drool off the walls, you need to be an attentive nanny. We keep “wipes” at hand, pretty much everywhere. When on-the-wall drool is wet, a damp paper towel will clean it off. Otherwise, Mr. Clean Magic Eraser (dampen the eraser-sponge, wet the drool, then wait a minute or so to come back and use the eraser to remove the drool). If you let this stuff build up, it’s depressing and daunting — so we make it a habit to “See some drool? Wipe it off.” My “Why they drool” theory is that dogs descended from English mastiffs — the largest and oldest breed in the world — are everywhere because Julius Caesar, et al, used them as “war dogs.” Yep, these “war dogs” went with invading troops and, like many soldiers, spread their seed among the conquered females. “These dogs can be seen in the ancient images relating to Babylonian relics way back in 2200 BC. During these times, the dogs we commonly used during wars”: List of mastiff breeds: Your dog drools by design: Relax. Enjoy knowing why your dog drools. Keep a wipe handy!

Question: When crate training a puppy, can he sleep in bed?
Answer: My pup/dog always has slept with me. We like being together. We like to cuddle. Folks who tell you it’s dirty and dogs carry disease and so on are people who are unwilling to keep a dog healthy, clean, vaccinated and vet-checked: They do not deserve to have a dog and should simply buy a stuffed animal, put it on the bed, and pretend. If you want your pup to sleep in bed with you, your puppy will be happy, happy! But think about who’s being “crate trained”: You or your pup? You make the rules. You are the parent and he is the puppy. Be prepared for these things: #1 Your puppy is too young to have bladder control — so you must make sure he relieves himself before bed and during the night, etc. This is your job, not his. #2 Be prepared for your puppy to want to cuddle up, including thinking it would be lovely to sleep on your head because he likes the way you smell, etc. #3 You choose where to let him sleep in bed with you. But, he’s going to want to move around and change places during the night — that’s what pups and dogs do — so he will move whenever he gets too hot or cold or whatever….He may end up sleeping at the end of your bed, with his eyes on the bedroom door, protecting you. This, too, is what dogs do. #4 Once you let your puppy sleep with you, he will decide that he always can. You should not let your pup jump off the bed — really, really bad for his joints and bones! You must prevent him from hurting himself (possibly permanently) by jumping up and hopping down by himself: You are responsible, not your pup! When my dog Trixie was a pup, she would put her front paws up on the bed, then look back over her shoulder at us, as if to demand: Well, come here and give me a boost up! (Oh, yes, she had come to expect help from us and knew we should hurry to do her puppy bidding. Expect this too: What once was a privilege becomes a right. Puppy power!) #5 When you wake up with your pup, immediately take him out to relieve himself. Then you can bring him back to bed to cuddle and play. A dry bed is a happier bed. One last thing to remember: Your puppy is going to grow. My little 10-pound+ puppy now weighs 150+. Her cute little sleepy sounds have turned into startling snores. When she moves around, so does the bed. So, be prepared because you are telling your pup he belongs in your bed. Tip: My dog has her own blankets: I spread one on top of the bed linens to be under her, so her doggie fur and dirty feet don’t matter, because our bed and her pillow are covered. If you want to do the same with your pup, you might want to spread some water-proof, absorptive pads under this blanket: One blanket is easier to replace/wash than a bedspread, etc. The other blanket is to cover her when she’s wet or cold (and to keep me from being either one, courtesy of my pup/dog). By the way, she has her own beds (baby-crib mattresses with washable crib sheets and such): One in our bedroom and one in our library where we work. She chooses when she wants to use them. Before she was safe to leave on her own by herself in our home, she had another bed — in her crate. Have fun and enjoy your pup!

Question: Puppy born with eyes open does that mean blindness?
Answer: Maybe the pup could face blindness. You need to act immediately to make sure your pup’s eyes are not exposed to light. Keep the whole litter and mom in a very, very dimly lit area. I do not think you could put a blindfold on the pup because mom would lick it off. Call your vet. At birth, a puppy's central nervous system is still developing, including their optical nerves. Because their optical nerves aren't fully developed, they're too delicate for bright light—which is why their eyes remain shut until the nerves are finished developing. What happens if you open a newborn puppies eyes? Remember, you should never force a puppy's eyes open. Every breed, litter and puppy within that litter will open their eyes at their own pace when they are ready. Forcing their eyes open before they are ready can lead to infection, eye damage and even permanent blindness.

Question: What is the best affordable puppy food?
Answer: YOU DO NOT HAVE TO FEED YOUR DOG PRICEY DOG FOOD. I KNOW AND OFFER PROOF OF WHAT I AM SAYING: Look at this Lab: First, as a young, energetic gal, with honey-blonde hair and then as an 8+-year-old greying lady. Same dog. Same gusto. Same healthy body. Happy, healthy, playful, active. Please also note her trim figure: We kept Cracker at her vet-approved weight. Our Lab “Cracker” is proof that good dog food does not have to cost a fortune. We fed Cracker food that was readily available at grocery stores and Walmart: We fed Iams and Purina. I recommend IAMS PROACTIVE HEALTH or PURINA ONE. Either one is first-class, regularly tested food, produced by companies of long-standing credibility. Our vets always have approved of these two fine dog foods. None has ever recommended “no grain” kibble (because some vets are worried about it). IAMS PROACTIVE HEALTH or PURINA ONE are always vet-recommended. We believe in dry dog food, which we use as treats as well as food. Dry dog food — softened with warm tap water and with something nice on top (like canned puppy food or canned chicken or tuna, etc.) — works perfectly for pups/dogs of every age. We start our pups on the same food that they will eat for the rest of their lives, simply moving from puppy to grown dog to senior, as their lives progress. If your dog will likely weigh 50 pounds or so, I would go with “large breed” puppy food. “Large breed” is balanced to give your pup’s body the nutrients it needs. “Puppy food” adds special nutrients during the time it takes for your pup’s body to grow into itself. We feed “puppy food” for a year. Again, two trustworthy American brands that I have found to be good-quality and readily available are IAMS PROACTIVE HEALTH Smart Puppy Large Breed Dry Dog Food Chicken, and PURINA ONE Natural Large Breed Dry Puppy Food, SmartBlend Formula. (FYI: Walmart’s “Old Roy” is not recommended.) (I have serious doubts about “designer dogs” and “designer dog foods”: Both to me seem to appeal more to one’s ego, than to reason and worth.) We do not ever feed our dogs any treats made by any manufacturer: Dogs have died from “treats” and pig ears and such. Skip all of this! Instead, give your pup pieces of apple, carrots, frozen green peas, cooked and sliced sweet potato, etc. (We also keep small containers of our dogs’ dry dog food available to use as “treats” — our dogs view these “kibbles” as special and delightful, while we view their kibbles as safe, easy to keep on hand, fresh, and totally trustworthy. For us, it’s win, win!)

Question: Can you apply for an ESA letter before you get the animal?
Answer: Below is an answer that I offer to you because I honestly believe this lady knows what she is talking about: Stephenie Lee, Dogs Owner& Corgi Fans Originally Answered: Can you get an ESA letter online? A valid emotional support animal letter should come from a licensed mental health professional, including psychiatrists, psychologists, licensed clinical social workers, psychiatric nurses, licensed professional counselors, and other licensed therapists. The final rule: Defines a service animal as a dog that is individually trained to do work or perform tasks for the benefit of a person with a disability; No longer considers an emotional support animal to be a service animal; Requires airlines to treat psychiatric service animals the same as other service animals; SO: TO FLY ON AN AIRLINE, THE WORDING NEEDS TO BE A “PSYCHIATRIC SERVICE” ANIMAL Schedule an appointment with your health care provider. You could simply go to your primary care physician, or to any doctor. However, the person in the best position to write an ESA letter for you is the mental health professional who is treating you for your mental disorder, as he would be familiar with your health condition and save some time to make the ESA letter. Make sure the online letter is written by a licensed doctor. Describe specifically your need for the letter. In the US, ESA letters may be used for 2 distinct purposes. Either you want to bring your animal with you in the passenger cabin of an aircraft, or you want to be allowed to keep your animal with you in no-pets housing. For example, if you have anxiety and a pathological fear of flying, your therapist might be able to write you an ESA letter to have your animal in the cabin of an aircraft. Explain how your pet eases the symptoms of your disorder. While your health care provider doesn't have to name the disorder you have, they do need to be able to describe how your animal helps you manage your symptoms. Often, the animal provides a calming effect. Provide your health care provider with a sample letter. You can find sample letters online to make sure that your health care provider includes all the information necessary for a valid ESA letter. Generally speaking, the letter must state that you have been diagnosed with a recognized mental disorder and that your ESA eases the symptoms of that disorder.Note that the ESA letter is only one of the paperwork when you rent a house or travel with your ESA. Make sure you have prepared other documentation and use them within the expired date. Lastly, the laws governing emotional support animals vary from country to country. See the ESA rules in the U.S here: Emotional Support Animals - Laws, Qualification & Certification Check out if your ESA letter can apply in your country or province.

Question: Is a Newfoundland dog the same as a saint bernard?

Both are “working dogs”: The Newfoundland rescues sailors from the North Sea and the St. Bernard rescues skiers, or so the stories go. These are both strong-willed, strong dogs. If I had a choice, I would always go with a Newfoundland over a St. Bernard because “Newfies” are pretty generally sweet-natured, easy-going dogs, although they, too, have been overbred and often have health issues. St. Bernards can be aggressive with people they don’t know, which appears to be an increasing concern, as well as health issues. Likely overbreeding is at fault here, too. Both breeds have to be “independent thinkers”, like our English mastiff service dogs have to be, because they must be willing and able to overrule people who are about to make big-time mistakes. This means that whoever chooses to have either dog join his/her family must be willing to work with and train the dog. It’s best to start with a puppy because these dogs get big, big and do it quick, quick. Gentle training with love is the way to go with these dogs. Trying to overpower a dog like these will result in an angry big dog who will be blamed for whatever happens, when it is man’s fault for not being a proper dog-parent. Done right, trained carefully and made to be one of the family, these dogs are loyal, loving companions. Question: I’ve been teaching my lab puppy to sit but he only sits whenever I give him a treat. He never sits when I ask him to other than when he gets a treat, why? What am I supposed to do?
Answer: This is the “oops” about giving a treat: No treat, no performance. Well, drat! So, let’s fix “sit”: #1 You know that your pup knows the word “sit” and what he is expected to do, right? If yes, then proceed. If not, go back to step one: Say “Dog’s name” SIT: One hand on his hips, the other holding a treat (to bring up to his nose, then up and back high over his head), easing him into sit as you gently push his hips down. Make certain your pup knows what is expected of him. #2 You have to be in control of the situation. Period. Do not ask your pup to do something when you can not enforce the command. #3 What I would do is take my pup for a short walk in the house. Yep, a gentle walk — on a leash. Put the pup on your left and use both hands: Hold the leash with your right hand, then loosely drape across to your left hand. Use your left hand to gently and firmly control your pup. As you are walking, slow down, then pull back on the leash (not up) as you stop and say “Dog’s name” SIT. If you need to, move up closer to your pup, so you can put your hand on his hips and gently push down toward the “sit” as you say the command. Be encouraging. Be happy, happy when he sits: Praise and pet him, “Atta boy! Good puppy! Do this a couple of times, then quit on a high note. Pups can handle about 5+ minutes of working, then need to stop and rest. Let the lesson sink in. Do this two or three times a day, with praise, petting and “Atta boys!” Treats are to be given to please you by making him happy, happy — not as a pay-off for behaving as he must learn to do in order to earn the freedom that you two will enjoy when you can take him everywhere. Have fun! (And remember, Labs are silly puppies until they are at least 3–4 years old. Be patient and kind. Your Lab is a treasure!)

Question: Are either PetSmart or Petco good for training dogs? I'm on social security and private trainers are way too expensive for me. Thanks very much for your help.
Answer: First, please read the responses by Brenda Lux who offers great ideas for finding good, inexpensive dog-training classes (and likely a group of new dog-folks friends) and the one by Terry Dinerman who discusses the prices of classes at Petco and Petsmart and more. Second, think about what you want for yourself and your dog. Make a written list of what you need from the class and why you need it. Third, let’s think about your dog: Do you have a big dog that you cannot control? We have two 150-pound+ English mastiffs. Without my husband, I could not have either one of these dogs. Yes, I have had dogs all my long life, have had superb dog-training classes, and I know how to train my dog. But….I am a LOL (Little Old Lady) who has a very strong will (necessary with mastiffs who are bred to protect, so will overrule something they think is wrong), but has the sense to know that even in my twenties I was never strong enough to stop and hold a mastiff. Do you have a small enough dog that you can pick up and carry if you needed to? If so, then this means you are physically strong enough to handle your dog. Do you simply lack confidence in how to train your dog? Now, my bottom-line advice: #1 I have taken classes at PetSmart and have found them wanting, even for basic obedience. The instructors emphasize “treats” — food “rewards”. Using a treat to help guide a dog into a sit is not unreasonable, but to use food as a reward for good behavior totally bypasses the only reward a person with a dog will always have: Approval, such as petting and “Good, girl!” etc. For me and my dog, a PetSmart class was only used to socialize my pup with other pups. These people are not equipped to help you with a difficult dog. #2 If you have a “difficult dog” that is out-of-control and you can’t handle, then I suggest you find that dog another home. You need a dog that can’t hurt you and that brings you only pleasure. You are on Social Security, so you may be like me (old), so give yourself a break: Get an easy, cuddly, happy dog that you can handle. #3 Dog training is like training a child: It starts at home, from the beginning and is reinforced constantly. So, my list of what I want my dog to do is quite basic: Come, sit, stay, heel, etc. That’s it. Look at your list: I bet it’s similar to mine. #4 Train your dog yourself. Decide what you want your dog to do, then decide how it is best for you to accomplish this: YouTube is free (See what other folks are doing. Does it work for you? If so, start doing it.) Decide on the words you want to use (COME, Doggie! and so forth) and use them, again and again. All the time. A little puppy 8+ weeks old needs to be loved and guided and taught from the beginning how to be welcome anywhere you two want to go. Your pup/dog needs a walking leash to attach to his collar/harness that is light enough for you to start using immediately. For “treats” we use bits of our dog’s kibble (dry food) that we keep in readily available containers wherever we might want to reward our dog for making us happy, happy. Praise, petting and “Atta girl” is how our dogs are trained, but we choose to give them extras from time to time. We do not trust commercially available treats. #5 Teach your pup/dog, using his/her name. Let your pup/dog gently get used to things (Example: With a leash, first put it on your pup and let him/her get comfortable wearing it, then show how it’s used: In your home, let the pup/dog take you somewhere, then do the reverse. Always gentle, always kind. Your pup/dog will learn what the leash is for: Walking together. Do this again and again. See?) TRUST YOURSELF. TRUST YOUR GOOD SENSE. TRUST YOUR KINDNESS. YOU CAN TEACH YOUR DOG YOURSELF. BE KIND WITH YOURSELF AND YOUR DOG.

Question: What is the prognosis for a 9-year-old mixed Yorkie-Bichon Maltais dog who has just been diagnosed with pancreatitis?
Answer: EVERY CASE IS DIFFERENT. PLEASE READ THE AKC EXPERT EXPLANATION BELOW. FIRST, READ THIS: A canine researcher’s case study: her own dog Caroline Coile, Ph.D is the Nutrition and Health columnist for AKC Family Dog and a two-time AKC Canine Health Foundation Award winner. Pancreatitis is a subject Coile knows well, not only as a professional canine researcher and writer, but because her dog, a Saluki named Beanie, went through the difficult and stressful experience. Here she shares her story: Beanie, unlike most Salukis, loves to eat. But one day, after eating his very favorite treat—a flaky biscuit—he vomited it up. He was standing with his back kind of hunched. I gently pressed on his abdomen, and he yelped. Out came the thermometer, which told me his temperature was 103 degrees. While I was calling the veterinarian, he vomited again, then lay down in a corner. We were in the car within minutes. The veterinarian palpated his abdomen, which was definitely tender; took his temperature, which was still high; and drew blood. Beanie received pain medication, antibiotics, and intravenous fluids to combat fluid loss and came home with strict instructions not to eat that day. Eating anything—or even smelling food—could have caused his pancreas to secrete enzymes and slow its healing. He could lick ice cubes, and then drink a bit of water. The next day, he was allowed to eat about six tiny meals of low-fat, high-carbohydrate food. This meant rice, potatoes, or pasta. Overcooking these starchy foods makes them easier to digest. We would boil one cup of white rice (not instant rice) in four cups of water for 30 minutes to make a rice porridge called congee. We gradually added in protein sources, such as skinless chicken breast, low-fat cottage cheese, or boiled hamburger meat. When feeding a dog with pancreatitis, it’s important to cook all the food even if you normally feed a raw diet. Because the dog’s gut is compromised, it’s necessary to remove fat and destroy bacteria. After a week, Beanie progressed to a veterinary prescription diet for dogs with pancreatitis. He hated it. Many dogs with a history of acute pancreatitis must be on a special diet for the rest of their lives. If they don’t like the pancreatitis diet, a low-fat weight loss diet often works just as well. Since obese dogs are more prone to pancreatitis, they need to lose weight anyway. Even if a high-fat meal didn’t cause the initial bout, it can trigger a recurrence once the dog has had pancreatitis. After a month, Beanie was able to gradually transition back to his old diet, minus the high-fat treats. Eventually, he even got his breakfast biscuits—but no more butter. He never had another bout of pancreatitis. “Unfortunately, once a dog has had a bout of pancreatitis, the chance of recurrence is high. You best defense against a repeat appearance of this unwelcome intruder is a two-pronged approach: Be on the look-out for the warning signs and control the things you can. Don’t let your dog become obese (exercise is good for both of you), follow your vet’s feeding instructions strictly, and, when relevant, administer your dog’s medication faithfully. Mild cases of pancreatitis usually have a good prognosis. Severe cases have a more guarded prognosis, due to the potential for systemic complications.“

I KNOW AND OFFER PROOF OF WHAT I AM SAYING: Look at this Lab: First, as a young, energetic gal, with honey-blonde hair and then as an 8+-year-old greying lady. Same dog. Same gusto. Same healthy body. Happy, healthy, playful, active. Please also note her trim figure: We kept Cracker at her vet-approved weight. Our Lab “Cracker” is proof that good dog food does not have to cost a fortune. We fed Cracker food that was readily available at grocery stores and Walmart: We fed Iams and Purina. I recommend IAMS PROACTIVE HEALTH or PURINA ONE. Either one is first-class, regularly tested food, produced by companies of long-standing credibility. Our vets always have approved of these two fine dog foods. None has ever recommended “no grain” kibble (because some vets are worried about it). IAMS PROACTIVE HEALTH or PURINA ONE are always vet-recommended. We believe in dry dog food, which we use as treats as well as food. Dry dog food — softened with warm tap water and with something nice on top (like canned puppy food or canned chicken or tuna, etc.) — works perfectly for pups/dogs of every age. We start our pups on the same food that they will eat for the rest of their lives, simply moving from puppy to grown dog to senior, as their lives progress. Since your Lab will likely weigh 50 pounds or so, I would go with “large breed” puppy food. “Large breed” is balanced to give your pup’s body the nutrients it needs. “Puppy food” adds special nutrients during the time it takes for your pup’s body to grow into itself. We feed “puppy food” for a year. Again, two trustworthy American brands that I have found to be good-quality and readily available are IAMS PROACTIVE HEALTH Smart Puppy Large Breed Dry Dog Food Chicken, and PURINA ONE Natural Large Breed Dry Puppy Food, SmartBlend Formula. (FYI: Walmart’s “Old Roy” is not recommended.) (I have serious doubts about “designer dogs” and “designer dog foods”: Both to me seem to appeal more to one’s ego, than to reason and worth.) We do not ever feed our dogs any treats made by any manufacturer: Dogs have died from “treats” and pig ears and such. Skip all of this! Instead, give your pup pieces of apple, carrots, frozen green peas, cooked and sliced sweet potato, etc. (We also keep small containers of our dogs’ dry dog food available to use as “treats” — our dogs view these “kibbles” as special and delightful, while we view their kibbles as safe, easy to keep on hand, fresh, and totally trustworthy. For us, it’s win, win!) Labs are a joy! You two are in for a happy, happy time!

Question: Has anyone’s dog reacted differently to you after you had the COVID vaccine? My consistently lovable Austrian Pincher, Diana, recoiled terribly from me for a few hours after I had the first shot.
Answer: We have two English mastiff medical service dogs, whose job it is to know what’s going on with my husband and me. They sleep with us, cuddle up with us, and are our intimate companions who usually go everywhere we go. When we went to get our COVID vaccines, we left our dogs at home because they are very large (Our Southern gal Trixie weighs a trim 150+ pounds, while her brother Shomer is closer to 200.), so bringing two big dogs to the place old folks like us were having shots seemed unnecessary and an added tension for most people. Both dogs greeted us with their usual enthusiasm when we returned from taking both shots. They were happy, happy. Their loving support remained the same and they went in with us as usual for our afternoon naps. So, I wonder if your loving Diana somehow picked up on something that was not obvious to you. Given our dogs’ behavior and your description of Diana, I cannot believe her reaction was caused by the COVID vaccine: It must be something else. You wrote her reaction lasted “a few hours”… Perhaps you brushed against something that she could smell and you couldn’t, but I find that less likely to believe than the possibility that her feelings got hurt. Could it be that Diana was telling you that your going off without her to get something done that worried you was not a good thing. Your little Diana loves you. She wants and needs to protect you. Maybe her behavior was the only way she has to tell you — by showing you — how she feels. I am proud of you for getting your COVID vaccine because not only are you saving your own life, you are being an American patriot. Thank you.

Question: What breed of dog is best for protection and companionship while traveling in an RV?
Answer: Kat, in answer to your question about RV traveling with a dog that offers protection and companionship, I have what I believe to be a reasoned answer: As a life-time dog owner with 10 years experience as a full-time RVer traveling with a husband, a Jeep, a motorhome and a dog, I believe that you can benefit from my advice. We had a Labrador retriever when our house flooded and we decided to chuck the whole house bit and, as Dinah Shore’s Chevrolet ad suggested, “See the USA!” We bought a used 39′ gas RV and a Jeep we could tow 4-wheels-down, sold our house, put everything we wanted to keep in long-term storage and set out. Our Lab, Cracker, of course went with us. Because we found we were having such a good time, we chose to make a 5-year minimum commitment to “go for it”, bought a new 39-foot diesel RV that could comfortably tow our Jeep, and went RVing with our “part-of-our-family” dog. Labs are welcome in RV parks, but so very many dogs are not. Any dog that looks big and mean is not welcome. Period. RV parks are private property and must have rules to maintain safety, cleanliness, comfort, etc. Any dog that scares people or is not cleaned up after on potty walks or is allowed to bark incessantly can cause real trouble. Every RVer who has a dog needs to plan for the dog’s care. Dogs require a lot of extra effort: We already knew that Cracker (of throw-the-ball, let’s go swimming! fame) needed lots of exercise, so we made it a point to find safe places to take her. Since we used our RV as basecamp and toured in our Jeep, she went with us everywhere. We got her out almost every time that we got out to look at something, etc. If taking her was inappropriate, we arranged for her care (a dog walker, etc.). Although she was a happy, blonde, “want-to-play-with-me” 45-pound Labrador retriever, still some folks were afraid of her: Big, scary dog! Now we live in a house and have a 34′ gas RV with 3 slides and do not tow a vehicle. If we want/need a car, we rent one. But not towing (so 34′, not 60′ long) is more relaxing, let’s us go and see (sitting much higher up than in our Jeep) many more places on the road, and is a lot more practical for us and our dogs. Now we have two big, blonde (“fawn”) English mastiffs. These 150-pound+ dogs tend to scare most people, so they wear “Medical Alert Dog” vests and are kept on lead and usually at heel. Traveling with them requires a lot more work and hassle. Luckily, mastiffs were bred to lie around and like to rest a lot, so walking them is generally enough. Now, to answer your question: I will use myself as an example. As a LOL (Little Old Lady) getting a dog and a small RV for my use, I would get a little dog that liked me and that I liked. The breed doesn’t matter because any dog will bark and give warning of (and to) an invader. Our big mastiffs know that no dog can defend against a serious attacker: Only people can do that. I depend on good sense, careful planning and being prepared to defend myself and my dog. I would love to have a Cavalier King Charles spaniel. This breed’s health issues worry me, but, as a LOL, why not get exactly what I want? (As a teenager, I read about “Susan” — a big mastiff who went everywhere with her newspaper-reporter mistress. Now I have Trixie, my English mastiff, who suits my lifestyle and makes me happy, happy.) So, when the time comes, why shouldn’t I go for the only other dog I think I’d really like to have? AKC Cavalier King Charles Spaniel Dog Breed Information: “The Cavalier King Charles Spaniel is an active, graceful, well-balanced toy spaniel, very gay and free in action; fearless and sporting in character, yet at the same time gentle and affectionate.” Consequently, why don’t you do the same? Think about what kind of dog you have always wanted and get that breed. Find the dog that makes you happy, happy! I prefer to start out with a puppy because that way I will know who she is and how she has been taken care of, plus be able to gently train her from the start so that she knows how to conduct herself anywhere, any time, with anyone. My dog would go with me everywhere because I want her and she wants to be with me. And yes, my dog will do her very best to protect me, as I will with her. We protect who and what belongs to us. Best wishes for every joy with your RV and your dog.
