Question: How can inbreeding cause genetic mutations among dog breeds?
Answer: Yours is an intriguing question and I learned a lot in trying to answer your “How can inbreeding cause genetic mutations?” Your use of the word “cause” freaked out some folks, but I think I understand that you want to know how in the world we humans are managing to destroy the very dog breeds we are so carefully breeding. Here’s a classic example: Inbreeding has destroyed the English bulldog's genetic ... www.newscientist.com › article › 2099278-inbreeding-... “Jul 29, 2016 — Inbreeding has destroyed the English bulldog's genetic diversity. The future looks dire for the English bulldog, one of the most popular – and illness-prone – dog breeds in the UK and US. Among other problems, English bulldogs have difficulty breathing, moving and mating.” It would appear that we’ve done this bulldog “inbreeding” so long and so well that all our bull dogs are fouled up. We have destroyed any possibility of restoring genetic diversity. Oops! Yep, breeding too close to the family tree often causes a dog with a recessive or mutated gene to be bred with another dog who has the same recessive or mutated gene and, voila! Now this recessive or mutated gene is dominant in the offspring. Another “Oops!” Perhaps it is easier to see in people: INBREEDING IN HUMANS Eugene Ochap Genetics 535 3-22-04 ... “Inbreeding was very common among the royal families of Europe, and it has been linked as the cause of the widespread number of cases of hemophilia in the families.” “Queen Victoria of England, who ruled from 1837-1901, is believed to have been the carrier of hemophilia B, or factor IX deficiency. She passed the trait on to three of her nine children. Her son Leopold died of a hemorrhage after a fall when he was 30.” History | National Hemophilia Foundation The Russian revolution was in part caused by “inbreeding” because the only son and heir to the Russian throne Alexei had “inherited hemophilia from his mother Alexandra, a hereditary condition that affects males, which she had acquired through the line of her maternal grandmother Queen Victoria of the United Kingdom.” Alexei Nikolaevich, Tsarevich of Russia - Wikipedia TMI about genetics and hemophilia: “As Victoria’s family showed no symptoms of the disease, it is believed that a spontaneous mutation on an X chromosome in either a parent at the time of the queen’s conception or the queen herself during her lifetime led to the introduction of the disease into the British royal family. “We now know that the disease is a genetic disorder located on the sex-linked X chromosome. The trait is recessive, meaning that women, with two X chromosomes, must inherit the mutation from both mother and father for the disease to appear. Otherwise, they remain silent carriers, increasing the likelihood of passing the disease down to their sons, who only have a single X chromosome and thus incur a fifty percent chance of contracting hemophilia even if their father is not a carrier, as was the case with Victoria and Albert.” Royal blood: Queen Victoria and the legacy of hemophilia in Europe Well, double “Oops!” But perhaps with our new scientific progress in genetics all is not yet lost: First of all, we are only at the beginning of trying to understand genetics. Think about it: We only discovered the DNA helix in 1962: “The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1962 was awarded to James Watson, Francis Crick and Maurice Wilkins for their discovery of the molecular structure of DNA”. Although that was 60 years ago, our DNA research is hampered by restrictions both ethical and political: In 2020, Scientists Grapple with US Restrictions on Fetal Tissue Research and New U.S. ethics board rejects most human fetal tissue research proposals. It was just last year that we discovered a way to slice and dice DNA: Oct 7, 2020 — Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer A. Doudna have discovered one of gene technology's sharpest tools: the CRISPR/Cas9 genetic scissors ... Press release: The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2020 ... www.nobelprize.org › prizes › chemistry › press-release CRISPR/Cas9 is being used right now to fight the Covid pandemic: 8 tools that helped us tackle the coronavirus - C&EN cen.acs.org › biological-chemistry › infectious-disease “Jan 25, 2021 — To make COVID-19 vaccines, researchers insert DNA encoding the ... trigger the immune system to develop antibodies and T cells that target the coronavirus. ... Better known for its use as a gene-editing tool, CRISPR got attention amid the ...” Second, we are only now beginning to understand mutations: “These changes can be caused by environmental factors such as ultraviolet radiation from the sun, or can occur if an error is made as DNA copies itself during cell division. Acquired mutations in somatic cells (cells other than sperm and egg cells) cannot be passed to the next generation.Sep 17, 2020 What is a gene mutation and how do mutations occur ... Third, we have begun to see what we have done and are continuing to do to dog breeds. Here’s a scientific explanation: Dog Inbreeding, Its Consequences, And Its Quantification | Embark Bottom line, can we fix it? Maybe. After all, if we can engineer Covid-19 vaccines by slicing and dicing gene-sequences, it is very likely that we can fix dog genes, too. Thank you for asking this question. I have enjoyed my research and I certainly hope you do, too. Wishing you and yours stay safe, healthy and well, Leslie

Question: Is there therapy dog testing available in the south Florida area?
Answer: What do you mean by “therapy dog testing”? (Thank you to Kerry Krueger and Jane Somers, who both pointed out that a “therapy dog” is not a “service dog.”) If you are asking about dogs that can go into nursing homes, etc., then the American Kennel Club can guide you, whether or not your dog has an AKC pedigree. Here’s the AKC info: What Is a Therapy Dog? – American Kennel Club AKC Recognized Therapy Dog Organizations – American Kennel Club How To Earn The Title: Qualifications – American Kennel Club THESE ARE ON THE AKC LIST (OTHERS ARE LISTED, BUT THESE ARE SOUTH FLORIDA): “Therapy dogs” are not the same as “service dogs”: What Is a Therapy Dog? – American Kennel Club If you are asking about a service dog, then your dog does not need a special test to be classified as a service dog. Having a “service dog” is simple and you can do it yourself. We have two English mastiffs, one for my husband and one for me, that wear “Medical Alert Dog” vests (from Amazon) and go everywhere with us. They are both well-trained — by us. Our dogs are huge (150+ pounds), so it is imperative that they are always under our control. We are both stroke survivors, so our dogs can help us go up and down stairs, etc. Our dogs know the basics: Sit, stay, heel, etc. They know how to behave when they are “working” and their manner changes into professional mode when they are wearing their vests. A vest makes a difference, both to the dog wearing it and to the public. Seeing “Medical Alert” tells folks what to expect and how to act with us and our dogs. It puts everyone at ease, especially since our dogs are perfectly behaved. You can can make your dog a service dog or a medical alert dog yourself: #1 All you need is a dog that suits you and answers your needs. This can be a toy poodle to an English mastiff, the size is not important. How the dog makes you feel is important. #2 Train your dog in the basics ( Sit, stay, heel, etc.) and dog manners (No jumping, barking, etc.). Your dog must be under your control and behaving nicely. Do not let people mess with your dog — You must always be in control of your dog, yourself and the situation. #3 Buy your dog a vest that says your dog is “working” (“Medical Alert Dog” etc.) and let your dog understand that putting on the vest means “working,” so put the vest on your dog at every appropriate time. If you want your dog to be “certified” talk with your doctor (any doctor will do). Your goal is a simple letter stating that yours is a service dog. That’s it. The doctor does not need to say why your dog is a service dog. No one legally has a right to ask you why you need a service dog, only what this dog does for you. If some fool hassles you about your dog, a really great off-putting answer is “my dog can tell when I am about to have “a spell” and lets me know.” Do you really think someone will want to hassle you into having “a spell”? No. “Having a spell” can be getting irritated when someone hassles you about your dog. Find a nice dog, be a good trainer, and buy a vest.

Question: Will a German shepards ears stand up on their own?
Answer: All German shepherds are born with floppy ears. Puppies have not yet developed their cartilage, and so, their ears are still not matured enough to hold up their ear’s weight. After all, they have relatively big ears. Since puppies are yet to develop strong ear cartilage, floppy ears are often seen in the first year of a German shepherd. This is natural and studies say that teething contributes to the floppy ears. As the teeth break through the gums, calcium is also extracted, which results in softer ear cartilage. Despite the complexity, some owners refer to teething as the puppy funny ear stage. Either way, you’ll start seeing progress with their ears during the 6th to 14th week, when the calcium is gradually produced which makes the cartilage strong enough to hold the ears’ weight. In addition to this gradual change, you may also notice a difference in their behavior right after the teething stage. For example, their floppy ears may suddenly stand up when hearing a book fall into the floor. All the above is from German Shepherd Floppy Ears: Is it Normal? - AllShepherd For more info, including the fact that some breeders are now in-breeding floppy ears “because they are cute” read the article.

Name: Leslie Perry Runnels Isbell
Question: What is it like living in Montana?
Answer: Montana has a special lure for many people, as it did for me — during the 10 years I went there repeatedly — until I realized three big-deal things: #1 Montana means being up-close and personal with “nature.” I’m a Florida gal, so I know about snakes and gators and jellyfish, but Montana is vastly different: Folks had better understand that nature is dangerous. People get themselves killed quite frequently because of doing foolish things — often because of not knowing any better. Some examples: Most knowledgeable homeowners in Montana do not have plantings up close to their homes because plants make great places for mountain lions to hide in wait until a dog or a little child or someone else that looks tasty walks by. Reacting to a mountain lion requires vastly different actions than reacting to a bear. Not knowing about rutting season and when animals have babies that they will die or kill to protect and other basic rules of nature can cost a person his life. #2 Montana gets really, really cold and stays that way for a long time every year. “Wind chill” adds to the danger. Folks freeze to death in Montana. Those who do not understand “serious winter” should be very, very careful not to expose themselves to genuine harm. Having your car stall out — with no one in sight and no cell phone service — is courting Montana mid-winter death. Oops! #3 Most important to me: Montana is being destroyed. “Big Sky Country” has rapidly been overwhelmed by “development.” Fascinating small towns, each with its own personality and special attributes, have been replaced by big-box stores and shopping centers and big-deal-expensive intrusions of folks with too much money and too little appreciation of the once-unique character of Montana. For all of these reasons — with the third being of overwhelming importance — I have given up romantic dreams of living in Montana. The “real topper” is “climate change” = global warming. The last time I was in Missoula, Montana, where I had once hoped to live, I discovered that Glacier National Park is rapidly losing its namesake, that it was necessary to get up and out by 5 AM to go walking on Blue Mountain because summer heat in downtown Missoula daily got up to over 100 degrees by mid-morning, and that the smoke from the wildfires made it almost impossible to breathe. My inescapable conclusion? For many of us, “Montana” is gone.

Question: What are the top 3 daily frustrations/challenges of owning a puppy?
Answer: The three daily challenges of owning a puppy are: #1 Remembering that a puppy is like a human baby and needs a parent to protect and guide it. This means being a “parent,” not a “playmate,” and using every moment to help the puppy understand what the expectations are for your puppy to succeed anywhere you want to take your puppy. You are responsible for teaching your puppy, gently and carefully, the basic rules of doggie behavior: Come, sit, stay, heel, plus “No,” “That’s enough,” and “You’re free.” This teaching begins immediately and continues throughout the pup’s life = a seamless, easy, relaxed approach to controlling and making any pup/dog feel secure. (FYI our two 150+ pound English mastiffs, trained by us and living with us in our home, are in a photo at the end). #2 Knowing about “puppies” and your puppy and your puppy’s breed in particular, so that you can prove you are worthy of your pup’s love. This means that you know your puppy (like all babies) will sleep a lot, will need to be fed regularly and often, will need to be protected from ignorant folks who will want to play too much with your puppy and go too far, pushing your puppy to do things the pup should never be expected to do. This means no “Merry Christmas, pup” and such foolishness. This also means that you know what your pup’s breed is bred to do: Retrieve, pull a sled through the snow, lie around keeping watch over his/her master, etc. Expecting a pup to grow into doing something that is against its nature is like planning to marry someone to change that person into what you really want: Dumber than rocks. You need to know if your pup’s breed is by nature aggressive or laid back, a worker or a companion, etc. You also need to realize that growling at puppy and playing “rough” teaches your pup that this is OK and your pup can do it, too. You also need to know that it is highly likely your pup (because of being taken too soon from siblings and mom) does not understand that biting hurts because he has not been taught. Consequently, you must give your teething pup something to chew (even a clean, braided and knotted rag will do) that is not you. If your pup nips you, do not permit this to continue: “No!” and a quick, light swat on the pup’s fanny (never the face or the nose) should convey your message. These things are your responsibilities, not your pup’s. #3 Anticipating and responding to your puppy’s needs. A prime example: Puppies have bodies that are still developing. This means you need to take your puppy to the proper place to relieve itself: A puppy’s sphincter muscles will not allow a pup to “hold it.” Every time your pup plays or wakes up, it is your responsibility to protect the pup from “accidents.” This means regular, often opportunities for the pup to be in the right place and be praised for doing its business appropriately. Praise, help, gentle training and love are what you owe to your puppy. If you can’t see yourself doing this, then get a stuffed animal, not a pup. These are our English mastiffs, raised and trained by us since their puppyhood. Trixie is 8 and Shomer is still a pup. She weighs in at about 150 pounds and he will likely be about 175. Both make us happy and proud to take them anywhere: By the way, if you have a puppy who will be a large or giant dog like ours, please remember that as pups they are very fragile: Their tendons and ligaments are like rubber bands, able to stretch as the pup grows, and the “growth plates” at the ends of their bones can be damaged by too-rough play and cutting corners at a run, etc. Because of these considerations, we did not let either of our pups play with other dogs and we did not play roughly with them ever. We also do not allow someone to invade their personal space by petting without permission or to ruffle their ears (painful!) because folks often do not know how to behave. We protect our dogs and recommend the same to you. Best wishes for your earning total joy with your pup.

Answer: First, make certain you are feeding a “quality dog food” — not a pricey dog food, but a “quality dog food” — Your dog’s body may not be getting the nutrition it needs, so your dog may be eating way too much, trying to get the nutrients he is starving for. Question: Which dog should I buy as I have a 3 BHK flat with a big terrace? Should I buy a German Shepherd or Saint Bernard?

Question: Got a German shepherd and he has fear-based aggression to strangers. My trainer and vet both refer me to behavioral specialist which costs 800 AUD/3hrs for diagnosis. Is it worth that much? Does it fix any problems?
Answer: Heck, no! Skip the “behavioral specialist which costs 800 AUD/3hrs for diagnosis” because this is dumber than rocks. After spending your money and time, you will learn that your German shepherd is “aggressive” and likely needs to be either “put down” or “trained/referred” by this “behavioral specialist” for a zillion more dollars. You may have been born at night, but not last night. Think! You need to be your own “behavioral specialist”, starting with yourself: First, do you care enough about this dog to continue? If this were my dog and I loved this dog enough, I would get help training my dog myself. There are lots and lots of trainers out there, some of whom are competent. For example, take a look (via Amazon) at this training method that my husband (who once prepared dogs for the Kansas City Police canine corps has used) and highly recommends: The Koehler Method of Dog Training: William R. Koehler, R.T The Koehler Method of Dog Training: William R. Koehler, R.T. Yankie: 9780876055779: Amazon.com: Books I strongly suggest that you go to Amazon and read the descriptions of what others write. You can decide if this type of training might work for you and your dog. This is the re-issue of a serious, old-style dog training book that has been relied on for generations and is available on kindle ($3 US) and in book form, with various other bookstores, etc. also offering the book. “The Koehler method continues to be taught in both class and private training formats. The method is based in the philosophy that a dog acts on its right to choose its actions. Koehler explained that a dog’s learned behavior is an act of choice based on its own learning experience. When those choices are influenced by the expectation of reward, the behavior will most likely be repeated, and when those choices are influenced by the anticipation of punishment, they will most likely cease. Once the dog has learned that its choices result in comfort or discomfort it can be taught to make the correct decisions.” Give yourself a chance to look at what can be done and then to decide if you are able and willing to make such a commitment. Please remember, that an “aggressive dog” can lead to heartache and big-time expensive suits. Your dog has already been named by a vet and a trainer as “aggressive.” You must take action to protect yourself and your dog. You need a qualified, serious trainer who knows how to help you help yourself and your dog. Were I you, I would first look at the Koehler method (to familiarize myself with “real dog” training, so that another fool trainer couldn’t try to bamboozle me), then I would begin by getting in touch with the police/sheriff’s canine division to get help finding a competent trainer. After your dog has completed serious training with you and a truly competent trainer, that trainer can then assure you that your dog is under control and no longer qualifies as an “aggressive” dog. Best wishes for success in knowing, whatever your decision, that you have done your best. Leslie

Question: Which dog breed is good as my first dog to my house?
Answer: How about a poodle? Poodles are smart, loving, come in various sizes and colors, and generally are reasonably healthy and get along very well with people. Right now my dog Trixie is a 150+ pound English mastiff, a dog I had always wanted, but very much doubted I could ever have: A dog like this would have been unsuitable at any other time in my life. Now I am married to a man who is happy to help me train her, care for her, let her become my perfect service dog. We have a big home, a protected and fenced yard, and are delighted to share our lives with Trixie (and now have added “Shomer,” my husband’s English mastiff). In the past, as a teenager “my dog” was “Ginger”, a cocker spaniel (Yes, my mom ended up with her when I went off to college), then there was “Pace”, another cocker spaniel (Yes, I was working, so “my dog” got left at home too often for far too long), then there was “Cracker,” a Labrador retriever (This time both my husband and I were able to enjoy her: Retired with plenty of time to play, we lived on the water, he hunted, we had kids and dogs and lots of company — Perfect!). “Cracker” happily went with us when we decided to buy an RV and go “full time” to see the USA. Then came “Lady” an “All-American girl” and Hurricane-Katrina survivor: From a brutalized waif in a Louisiana RV park, Lady became “our dog” and then “my dog”: My mainstay after my husband died and I was left alone. Bottom line is to first consider yourself: What do you need and want from your dog? As you can tell, I ignored the fact that having a “welcome home” dog that was pretty and I could pet and cuddle when I was around was simply wrong. I failed to consider what a dog needs. So, I suggest you start with yourself: Your lifestyle, your home, how much time and interest you have to devote to a dog, whether or not you want to care for and groom and feed and walk and train a dog…. Then you will know what “my first dog” should be, that is if you still want one. Now, at the end of my life, I think that if I decided to have another dog after Trixie, I would choose a poodle that I could pick up and carry if I wanted/needed to, that I could brush and trim into a simple, easy, DIY “puppy cut” and that I could keep with me all the time, as my companion and friend. Best wishes for every joy, whether or not you decide to have a dog. Leslie

Question: We're getting a German shepherd puppy and my grandparents don't want her to stay in our home. We have a garden but I'm not sure if she can stay there all the time because I heard they are so social. The puppy I will get is about 3-4 months old?
Answer: Do not do this. Let this puppy go: You deserve better. The German shepherd puppy deserves better. “Our home” is how you describe living with your grandparents. Stop and think: They love you. They are caring for you. They deserve your love and your understanding. Don’t your grandparents deserve better than to have a puppy dog they don’t want in their home? FYI: No puppy dog who lives in the garden, not in your home, will love and protect you and your home. Why should the puppy dog care what happens to someone, some place that does not belong to the puppy dog? Tell your grandparents you do not want this puppy dog. One day, you will be able to have your own puppy dog in your own home. But first, I strongly suggest that you find out what it takes to be a good puppy dog “parent”: No longer are you free to follow your dreams where ever they lead because you must always plan for and take your puppy dog. Question: Can a collar hurt my anxious dog?
Answer: Yes, a collar can hurt your “anxious” dog. “Traditional collars can harm a dog's neck if it pulls hard on the leash or if a pet owner uses the collar to pull the dog around. ... Repeated stress on the neck can even lead to long-term medical issues—including damaging the thyroid glands and tissues around the neck area and salivary glands” 5 Ways Collars Can Harm Your Dog | PetMD Were I you, I would strongly consider getting my dog a harness. Yes, a harness: One that fits my dog perfectly, is soft and comfortable, and that can be worn whenever we go out together or, in fact, all the time. Then, I would use this harness to train my dog and myself how to use a leash. Here are three harness suggestions (all less than $20) that I would consider: Amazon.com : Voyager Step-in Air Dog Harness - All Weather Mesh, Step in Vest Harness for Small and Medium Dogs by Best Pet Supplies : Pet Supplies Amazon.com : Authentic Puppia Soft Dog Harness, Red - Medium : Pet Leashes : Pet Supplies Amazon.com : Bolux Dog Harness, No-Pull Reflective Breathable Adjustable Pet Vest with Handle for Outdoor Walking - No More Pulling, Tugging or Choking : Pet Supplies Your dog loves and wants to please you. Love your dog and show your dog just what needs to be done for you two to have fun together. Make learning fun! Here’s some advice from the AKC: Leash Train Your Puppy In 5 Easy Steps I would buy myself a matching leash that fit comfortably in my hand and was about 6′ long (so I could walk with my dog on my left side, with the handle of the leash held gently in my right hand and the leash draping across my front to be held in my left hand — to safely control my dog). With this set up, I would practice proper use of a leash. Any needed correction is made with a “quick snap and instant release” — a light, attention-getting “pop” — this takes practice to learn to do easily, gently and quick, quick. I would use my dog’s collar and our leash — along with a pocketful of dog kibble to use as treats, plus lots and lots of praise and petting — to teach “Come” and much more, gently and easily. Yes, I use voice commands. I also say my dog’s name first, then the command. I use “Good girl” and “Go free” (as a release so my dog knows she has done what I asked). I walk my dog with my dog by my left side and our leash held gently in my left hand (Again, with the leash draped across my front, so the handle is held in my right hand.) I first sit her on my left. (To “sit” her, stand with her to your left, at your side, then hold the leash down with your left hand, while offering a treat with your right — coming from in front of her eyes, then back over and above her head, saying “Trixie, sit” as she does so. With your left hand, guide and follow her down and back. Give her the treat. Good girl.) If we are just going for a walk — not at heel — I say “Trixie, let’s go.” Generally, I talk with her as we walk along together. If we are going to be “at heel” — I say “Trixie, heel” and step out on my left foot (on her side, so she can easily see my left leg and foot). We may go a few steps, then I may choose to “sit” her again. What we do is up to me. I am always in control. She is always safe when she is with me. See? Buy yourself a harness and a leash and have fun with your dog. Teach your dog with love and slowly eliminate the treats because you always have your gentle, happy voice and your petting with you, so you can reward yourself and your dog. Wishing you and yours stay safe, healthy and happy, Leslie

Question: Who are some of the best Labrador Retriever breeders in WA, Idaho, or Montana?
Answer: First, decide what you mean by a “Labrador Retriever”: What do you want to do with the dog (hunt, play with the family, use as a service animal, etc.). Are you aware that most Labs are “busy, busy” (throw the ball, throw the ball!), working dogs? And that a bored Lab will entertain itself doing “busy things” — like digging holes in the backyard and creating incredibly complex disasters? Labs need attention. Labs need love. Labs need to have real jobs (bring in the paper, fetch slippers, retrieve birds, etc.). Once you figure out what you want in your Lab — if you decide you really want a dog like this — then you can think about breeders. (And, please remember, just because a breeder is listed by the AKC or any other organization does not mean that breeder has any sort of genuine guarantee by that organization: The breeder has simply bought a membership and an ad.) Do your homework. Find out about Labs. Go visit breeders and check out their operations. Were I considering a Lab, I would demand that my pup come from a “family environment” — not pens “out back” — that my pup be socialized, friendly, happy, smelling of warm puppy and momma, and obviously delighted to be with me and mine. I demand a written guarantee of a full refund if my pup does not check out with our vet, where I will immediately take the pup. I demand that my puppy be at least 8 weeks old before I will take my pup away from his mom and litter mates. I demand that my pup have written proof of whatever it is the breeder is saying (AKC registration papers, vet records, family history, etc.) For me, a pup is a lifetime commitment. Both you and your pup deserve that you demand and expect at least this.

Question: What should I do about the thick gooey stuff that comes out of my two older dogs tear ducts? It is so thick and stiff that I can't get it off of them. I want to know both how to clean it off of them and how to prevent this discharge.
Answer: I think your dogs are both healthy and normal. Were these my dogs, each morning and throughout every day I would make it a practice to look at my dog’s eyes. Both of our dogs get “eye goop” — nasty-looking, heavy-duty “ick” — which I generally simply wipe off with my thumb (Yep, I know, gross!), then go wash my hands. If it’s more than one eye or more than one dog (which can happen here in south Louisiana, especially during Spring with plant-pollinating dust in the air), I dampen with warm tap-water a paper towel (or a Kleenex or toilet paper), hold each dog’s head firmly, and gently wipe away the “ick” — folding the towel to expose a clean, fresh surface each time for each eye. (Be very careful not to get the paper towel/Kleenex/toilet paper into contact with the eye — because all have wood fibers that can cause damage. This is why I prefer to use my thumb.) 5 Types of Dog Eye Discharge (and What They Mean) is an excellent, general guide to what is happening with your dogs. Relax. Enjoy your dogs. Watch over their healthy, normal eyes.

Question: Can I be a breeder for service dogs if I have one? I have a PSD and she has made my life 100 times better. I would love to help other people with disabilities. I have the time, money, and space.

Question: How do you prepare for a puppy’s first day at home?
Answer: First-Day Tips for Puppy Happiness: 1. Prepare for your puppy: Get him a blanket that will be his. (Suggestion: Wash it first--- no fabric softener --- some puppies are very sensitive.) A light-weight leash and a soft collar (not a choke chain --- That's dangerous and is only used during training sessions). Puppy food (the same kind that he's used to). A food bowl and a water bowl. Some toys (including a ball that's large enough not to get wedged in his throat --- never a golf ball!). Something soft to chew on and pull (An old hand towel with a knot tied in the middle works well). A cardboard box (no top, just 3 sides) that he can curl up in on his blanket or a towel so that he can snuggle down and feel safe. 2. GET THE PUPPY IN THE MORNING so he can begin to get comfortable in his new home in the daylight. 3. If at all possible, PLAN TO SPEND THE ENTIRE DAY WITH HIM. This is the most important day of your new life together --- his homecoming. (Think about how the puppy feels: shocked and afraid, carried off by strangers, away from his mother and everything he's ever known, alone in a terrifying new world. He needs compassion and support.) 4. Bring his blanket with you, so that he can be on your lap or next to you in the car going home. 5. Spend the day letting the puppy get comfortable with you and his new surroundings. Play with your puppy, talk with him. 6. LET HIM REST. Protect him from too much excitement and stimulation, especially from outsiders. 7. Help him begin to feel safe, confident, and wanted. Puppy Tips from Cracker's Family: A puppy gets really tired, really fast, and bounces back quickly, too. He requires a lot of rest. Activities need to be divided into shortened segments that can be repeated frequently, especially when training your pup. Your pup will want to lick you. (It's a bonding" activity: He's making you his.) Whether you allow this licking or not (We do.) is up to you, but never ever allow him to nip or bite --- Puppy biting is not "fun" and is never acceptable. Substitute something that belongs to the puppy for him to chew. We highly recommend a gentle, good trainer at 3 to 4 months where you can go with the pup and work with him yourself. This is also a wonderful time for your pup to socialize with other dogs and people in a friendly, controlled environment. We enjoyed our training sessions and daily practice times very much. Choose your trainer carefully --- people-oriented, loving dogs must be trained gently with love (never Alpha-dog, dominance, and force). We suggest that you meet with your chosen trainer early on so that you can begin to teach your pup the correct commands (sit, stay, come) during your daily life before he goes to "puppy school." Sometimes there's no substitute for spanking --- as in when the puppy starts to chew the electrical cords --- here, an immediate and severe reprimand (a swat on the fanny and a strong "No") gets results, especially since the pup soon learns that this punishment is reserved for "really, really bad things." Remember, puppies must not be exposed to other dogs until they're old enough to have had all of their required inoculations; however, you and your pup can work together happily to help him learn the basics at home. HOUSE TRAINING: Pups have very little bladder control --- Their sphincter muscles just aren't developed yet, so they need all the help they can get from you to reduce the "mistakes" that are bound to happen. Yelling at the pup for defecating or urinating indoors is not effective: He can't help it. Frequent trips outside (as in immediately after he eats, drinks, wakes up, plays, etc.) and praise will rapidly teach him where it's acceptable to go to the bathroom. He'll soon know where he's supposed to go, even though he often may not be able to make it. We discovered that taking our pup out to the same general location in our yard, quietly repeating the word "busy," and praising her for going outside (whether or not the anticipated results occurred) proved very successful as she grew and gained more self-control --- although we did learn to be careful using the word "busy." We referred to our yellow Labrador “Cracker” as "Mrs. Leaky" until she was at least 12 weeks old because, if left to her own devices, she'd leave yellow "dimes" and "quarters" all the way to the outside door: By the time she realized she needed to go outside, it was too late for her to get there without "leaking."

MORE SAFE-TREAT-IDEAS: Here are 11 healthy dog treats from a veterinarian: 11 Healthy, Natural Treats for Dogs in Your Kitchen “Apples: An apple a day doesn’t necessarily keep the veterinarian away, and a whole apple would be a bit much for a dog anyway, but they are good for dogs just like they are people! Full of nutrients and fiber, these are great snacks. Just be sure not to let your pup have the seeds or the core. Green Peas: Frozen or fresh, green peas are good treats, and most dogs love them. Hand your dog a couple as training treats or even put some in their bowl. Easy-peasy! Carrots: Loaded with beta carotene and other vitamins, carrots are almost guaranteed to be in your kitchen anyway. Why not cut up some bite-sized pieces and use them as a healthy reward? Some dogs can be bad about swallowing without chewing (we’re looking at you, labs and beagles), so if yours is one, be sure that the carrot pieces are an appropriate size. Green Beans: Dogs can eat green beans too! Just be sure that cooked green beans aren’t seasoned. Plain, please. These are a great source of greens and fiber. Watermelon: Just like humans, most dogs love watermelon as a tasty, hydrating, and beneficial snack. Be sure to remove any seeds, and don’t give your dog the rind. Cooked Sweet Potatoes: Cooked sweet potatoes may not seem to smack of convenience, but since they keep well in the refrigerator, it’s actually really simple to roast up some extra to share during the week with your furry family member. It’s best to keep them plain. Do not give dogs raw potatoes of any kind. Bananas: We all know that bananas are loaded with healthy nutrients. Most dogs love them, too, so they are a natural choice that you probably keep handy all the time. Just be sure not to overdo it. Given their high sugar content, it’s best to give bananas to dogs in moderation. Broccoli: Cruciferous veggies have well-known health benefits, and broccoli is a good choice for pups. Feel free to give them a few small pieces as a treat. These can be raw, roasted, or steamed, just unseasoned please. Like humans, dogs often have an easier time digesting high-fiber foods that have been cooked, but either is safe. Cooked Squash: Cooked squashes are great natural treats for dogs! And since there are several kinds of squash that are safe for dogs, this is a good option year round. Butternut squash, yellow squash, or zucchini are all great. Even pumpkin! Just be sure to remove seeds, and for the butternut, the rind, as well. Strawberries: Strawberries are sweet little vitamin C nuggets that dogs love. Like bananas, they are high in sugar, so just keep that in mind when you decide how many to give. Blueberries: Like strawberries, blueberries are great, healthy, and easy little treats to share with your pup!”

Answer: It’s always the dog’s fault, isn’t it? Obviously, the dog attacked out of fear that your uncle would be hurt. Yep, this was wrong in this case, but your dog was way beyond the warning stage…. Ripping a man’s leg open is serious aggression and indicates to me that this is a big-deal thing that must be handled properly by your uncle. But did your uncle let his dog know that things were OK before your uncle went to greet the gardener? I wonder…. Too bad dogs can’t talk. By the way, consider this: The dog may know a lot more about your uncle’s gardener than you people do. Has the dog seen the gardener do something or take some action that the dog believes could hurt your uncle? I know I was very confused when a gal I had thought was my good friend came for an over-night at my house during high school. My cocker spaniel dumped on her pillow. Oops! Turned out my dog knew my friend better than I did because that girl viewed me as completion — never a good thing — and was downright mean. Instead of fussing, instead I should have hugged my dog. I wish you and yours stay safe, healthy and happy.

Question: How much does it cost to treat Cushing’s disease in dogs?
Answer: You have my every sympathy if your dog has been diagnosed with Cushing’s Disease. “Often owners report that their first clue that something might have been wrong was their dog wanting to go out at night to urinate. The disease causes extreme thirst, so a dog with CD tends to drink tremendous amounts of water and urinate frequently. As the disease progresses, dogs lose muscle and become weak. Owners might notice a thinning of the skin, lesions on the skin, and hair loss on the flanks, neck, and perineum. Obesity and lack of energy are also symptoms. Because it takes time — at least one year — for these symptoms to develop, and because the symptoms are often mistaken for common signs of aging, many dogs have the advanced form of CD before the owner even recognizes a problem exists. Certain breeds are at a higher risk of developing CD. The Poodle, Dachshund, Boston Terrier, Boxer, and Beagle are some breeds to watch. Almost all patients are older than eight years when CD develops. Prognosis for Dogs With Cushing's Disease The average survival time for a dog with CD is about two years, with only 10 percent of patients living beyond the four-year mark. This statistic, however, does not mean that this disease causes death. Because CD is most often diagnosed in geriatric dogs, most die of unrelated causes brought on by aging.” Cushing's Disease in Dogs – American Kennel Club Frankly, if my dog had Cushing’s I would reward my dog’s unconditional love for me with unconditional love for her by keeping her happy and comfortable, knowing she is loved until the time came when I needed to have the vet put her to sleep, with me with her, helping her go on to whatever’s next. I wish you and your dog the joy of being together and doing the right thing, whatever that is for you.

Question: What is wrong with getting a dog from a dog breeder?
Answer: There is absolutely nothing wrong with getting a dog from a breeder. But forget about trusting “breeders” and trust yourself. It is up to you to do your job as a “potential puppy purchaser” (3 P’s — amusing, but this is the only amusing thing about buying a pup). Bottom line is that if you want a dog/puppy, it will be a crap shoot as to what you will get — no matter how much you pay for it or what pedigrees it has. You have to go to work to find the right pup for you: You are putting “your heart on the line,” so please be careful and be kind to yourself. When we buy a pup, we buy only from an individual/a breeder. For us, a pup is a lifetime commitment: We insist on a happy, healthy, well-adjusted pup who comes from folks who take care to properly socialize the puppies. We go to see the litter, meet the mama-dog, and see for ourselves where our pup would come from. We insist on vet records and appropriate guarantees from the breeder. We immediately take our pup to our vet and have our pup thoroughly vet-checked. The breeder is all-important. The perfect pup is all-important. When we found the right breeder and the right pup, we knew. If you find a puppy or a dog who relates to you, wants to be with you and that you like, too, then go for it! Let me tell you about how we found Trixie, then about breeders and “breeds”: I have wanted an English mastiff since I was a teenager and read about “Susan” who went with her mistress, a newspaper reporter, everywhere, keeping her unbothered and not hassled. English mastiffs are very big, very serious looking, calm, laid-back, loving dogs, bred to guard and protect. Looking for an English mastiff, the breeder became the most important choice: Here in the USA, AKC-show-judges and back-hills-“Bubbas” are setting a new standard for English Mastiffs: Short legs, bulky bodies, “heavies” are in. We regard this as a travesty and destruction of this magnificent breed: Bred to be unhealthy, with bodies too big for their frames to support. THESE ARE OUR ENGLISH MASTIFFS, with strong, healthy, solid bodies maintained at their ideal weight. Trixie is the grown-up girl at the back. She weights 150+ pounds and has maintained her vet-approve weight for all of her 7+ years. Shomer, the boy at the front, is still a puppy but will weigh closer to 200 when he is fully grown. Ours are what we believe an “English mastiff” should be, but they are becoming increasingly difficult to find. For us the breed standards and the breeder are most important when finding our perfect pup. We use the internet, looking at various breeders to see what each was offering — and rejecting breeder after breeder, until we found a promising few. With Trixie, we had located her breeder via the internet, liked the look of the puppies and the full-grown mastiff parents, had spoken with the breeder via telephone and liked what she had to say, so we drove 400 miles (round-trip, Baton Rouge, LA, to Dallas, TX) to visit the breeder in person and inspect her pups. We liked what we saw with the breeder: Dogs on site, with free reign of the house; puppies clean, shiny, happy, puppy-smelling. Trixie’s dog parents were healthy and welcoming. These were well-adjusted, people-friendly dogs. Perfect! When we met Trixie, it was love at first sight, for both the pup and us. We paid for Trixie and then, 2+ weeks later when she was old enough, drove back to Dallas to bring our puppy home. We’ve been happy, happy! ABOUT BREEDERS: · Please note: Does being an AKC breeder and/or winning at AKC dog shows guarantee “ethical, selective breeding”? Absolutely not. · Note, too: When the American Kennel Society lists a breeder, the AKC is not guaranteeing the breeder, who may choose to sell you a sub-standard pup and send the pup home with you too soon (8 weeks, minimum), etc. · The AKC has destroyed many breeds, all in the name of “show dogs.” (Info below) Consequently, I do not trust any breeders. Period. ABOUT BREEDS: First, decide on the breed/breeds that you might want: · Remember that dog breeds have been bred by man to do certain things: Labrador retriever is “throw the ball” because retrievers “retrieve.” Hunters hunt. Fighters fight. Get it? (These are the dog’s instinctual behaviors.) · Do your homework. Read and pay attention to what real folks say about each breed. o Use Google to search for information dog breeds - Google Search o Dog Breeds - Types Of Dogs - American Kennel Club o All Dog Breeds - Complete List of Dog Profiles - DogTime; · Carefully decide, given you and your lifestyle, what you want your dog to do for you. What are you willing to do for your dog? This will help in deciding if there is a breed that suits you, your wants and needs. Second, please acquaint yourself with the fact that the AKC has destroyed many breeds, all in the name of “show dogs”: Avoid these breeds! Example: American cocker spaniels were bred as sports-hunting dogs. Yep, that poor creature trotting around the Westminster show ring with “feathers” hanging down to trip the dog up with its own hair, as it grotesquely pools on the floor, is a travesty. But this is all about winning the approval of show judges, not about dogs’ well-being. Another example: Remember “Rin Tin Tin”? This German Shepherd’s most famous TV pose is that of him standing with his front feet up on a rock formation. Breeders like that “arched back” look, so bred to get it: Now German Shepherds are cursed with weak backs and arthritis. Additionally, they have been so inbred that irreversible kidney failure and death is bred into many German Shepherds so that death comes by eight years old. For a real horror story look at the English bulldog — the canine mascot of the University of Georgia and the proud icon of the U.S. Marine Corps — totally ruined with no chance of a recovery because the gene pool is now judged insufficient. “The future looks dire for the English bulldog, one of the most popular – and illness-prone – dog breeds in the UK and US.” Inbreeding has destroyed the English bulldog's genetic diversity www.newscientist.com › article › 2099278-inbreeding-has-destroyed-... Bulldogs Are Dangerously Unhealthy, But There May Not Be Enough Diversity in Their Genes to Save Them ... www.smithsonianmag.com › science-nature › bulldogs-are-dangerous...“Decades of breeding have accentuated the traits that make up the dog's distinctive and wildly popular look, but compromised its health (Can the Bulldog Be Saved?) in the process. Now, the first comprehensive genetic assessment suggests that the bulldog no longer has the genetic diversity left for breeders to raise enough healthy animals to improve its overall outlook.” How 100 Years of Breeding Ruined Ten Popular Dogs - The Dogington Post (The 10 dogs in this “Ruined” article are the bull terrier, chow chow, basset hound, boxer, English bulldog, dachshund, German shepherd, pug, St. Bernard, Shetland sheepdog.) Wishing you and yours stay safe and healthy and happy,

Koehler, R.T. ... www.amazon.com › Koehler-Method-Dog-Training Another dog-person writes “I've always had dogs and always obedience train them. Koehler's method works and Bleeding Hearts will bad mouth his method but if you love your dog…” Descriptive overview: “Strictly following the model set out in the “Koehler Method of Dog Training”, some 50 years later, the Koehler method continues to be taught in both class and private training formats. The method is based in the philosophy that a dog acts on its right to choose its actions. Koehler explained that a dog’s learned behavior is an act of choice based on its own learning experience. When those choices are influenced by the expectation of reward, the behavior will most likely be repeated, and when those choices are influenced by the anticipation of punishment, they will most likely cease. Once the dog has learned that its choices result in comfort or discomfort it can be taught to make the correct decisions.” These two excellent approaches to training your pup/dog will give you what you need to feel comfortable and know that you are giving your Rottweiler what it takes for both of you to enjoy your life together. You need to be willing and able to be a “parent” to your loyal, loving, strong-willed, big dog. Yours is a great dog! Wishing you and yours stay safe, healthy and happy, Leslie

Question: How can I make my dog more happy each day?
Answer: Find out what your dog likes and do it! Huh? Yes, let’s think about this: My English mastiff — bred to stay with and protect — likes to be with me. Trixie likes to lie about, get petted and talked to, go everywhere I go and stick to me like glue. She has a big ball with a handle on it — designed to entertain a horse in his stall — perfect for a gal who weighs 150+ pounds. But, she will play with me and enjoy her ball for 5 minutes or so, then she quits. Enough is enough. OK. We quit. Both of us are happy, happy. With my Labrador retriever — a happy-go-lucky breed designed to fetch (and fetch and fetch!) birds for hunters, balls thrown by owners, and loves to swim — Cracker was happy playing and fetching and running about with kids, etc. She loved going out in the boat, could climb a ladder to get back up on the pontoon boat, and enjoyed looking at Florida wildlife — no bark, just look. Great fun! See? What is your dog bred to do? If your dog is a “mix” as my Gumbo Gal Lady was, then do things you like and see if your dog likes them, too. Lady liked to ride in the car, especially if she could see and smell cows….OK. She liked to “hunt” and could “sprong up” over tall brush like a comic-character…OK. She liked to be petted and cuddled and talked to…OK. Together, we had a wonderful time. Trust yourself and your dog. Love one another. Have fun. Remember, your dog is already a winner because you care about pleasing your dog!

Question: What animals are good for stress? I can’t get a dog or a cat due to allergies. I recently got a ferret because I herd they were best for reducing stress. Not sure if it’s my ferret but that’s just not the case for me. Anyone have ideas?
Answer: Yes. Spend a couple of hundred dollars on setting up and getting ready to enjoy a fresh-water aquarium. Put it where you can see and enjoy your aquarium, with its colorful background, lighted cover illuminating the interior and its interesting fish-friends. Yes, I know that salt-water fish are exciting with vibrant colors and such, but they are down-right difficult to maintain properly. Fresh water fish are much easier and are very, very interesting. Take the time to figure out what you are doing. Get your aquarium all set up (absolutely level, very important) with placement you can enjoy, with a happy background (taped to the outside back of the aquarium, so it’s easy to change with your mood), and with everything else set and ready (fake plants, gravel, something decorative that the fish can hide in and play with, etc.), along with the water filter and aerator to help keep your fish safe and happy. Make sure to let everything get settled in, clean and safe, with water that’s fresh and also safe. Wait a couple of days to be sure. Then you will be ready for your fish-friends: Do not buy a Beta (handsome, with full, spreading tails) unless you plan for a one-fish aquarium. Betas will kill and eat everyone else and will destroy one another. Betas create a deadly environment, so do avoid them unless you enjoy watching fish kill each other. This is happening right now with our US Senate, where Republicans are the Betas: Knowing the outcome that is already killing our people, this may be fascinating, but it’s horrifying. For color, choose some pretty goldfish, which will swim about midway up (in the water level in the tank). For schooling interest, buy a bunch of neons, which will swim happily back and forth, slightly higher than the gold fish. After they are set up and getting along fine, buy yourself a plecostomus, which will happily suck around, cleaning the goop off the aquarium walls, enjoying itself eating algae and such. You will need to have at least a 20 gallon aquarium to have a “Mr. P,” whose family originated in the rivers of the Amazon jungle in South America. I honestly believe he was my favorite fish because mine got to be a big fish, who went about his business, eating and eating and cleaning and cleaning, without bothering anybody, just having his own good time. Wonderful! Once your aquarium is set up, just relax and enjoy it — other than feeding my fish (never too much, which only gets things out of balance), I did nothing. A balanced aquarium takes care of itself. Watching and caring for your fish can be fun, relaxing and mind-relieving. Wishing you stay safe, healthy and happy, Leslie

Question: Is it okay to feed a dog cooked chicken meat with bones or does it have to be boneless meat?

Question: What Illinois laws or significant reasons can I tell my autistic friend to convince him that neutering his bull-terrier pup ESA (Emotional support Animal) is the best thing for his pup? He has ESA letter from his PCP.
Answer: About neutering a bull terrier: Although there is no 100% definite answer, it is often suggested that you should have your male Bull Terrier neutered after he has reached the age of puberty. This is thought to have long-term health benefits, as well as helping to prevent behavioural traits, such as marking and aggression. When Should I Spay or Neuter My Bull Terrier? - Tailster Blog Neutering Your Male Dog – Pros and Cons: Good reasons to neuter your male dog You can call it neutering or castrating, or de-sexing. All three terms refer to removal of the testicles so your male can't breed or sire puppies. A dog who is NOT neutered is also called intact. Neutering reduces leg-lifting and marking territory. Intact males, driven by testosterone, usually lift their leg when they pee. This is called "marking" their territory. The higher they spray their urine, the more impressive they appear to other dogs. Some intact males become obsessed with marking territory and will tow you toward every tree and telephone pole. Some dominant bossy males will even mark inside your house. Now, neutering isn't a cure-all, because testosterone is also produced elsewhere in the body, not only in the testicles. Many dogs, even when neutered, will still lift their leg, but less obsessively. However, a dominant bossy attitude will need to be addressed through Respect Training. Neutering reduces dominance and aggression. This is due to the reduction of testosterone, but remember, NOT ALL testosterone is removed by neutering. If your dog has inherited his dominance or aggression, or if caused by improper socialization or training, then neutering by itself won't be enough. Since testosterone fuels the fires of many unwanted behaviors, neutering is the best first step. But other causes of dominance and aggression still need to be addressed through Respect Training. Neutering reduces the risk of your dog being attacked by other male dogs. Even if your dog isn't aggressive himself, being intact makes him a target for other intact males who might see him as a potential rival. Neutering helps re-focus your dog's attention. Intact males often pay too much attention to other dogs, as they may be on the lookout for potential mates and rivals. Neutering can break your dog's over-focus on other dogs and Respect Training will teach him to re-focus on YOU. Neutering can reduce sexual behaviors. Intact dogs are more likely to hump other dogs, pillows, stuffed animals, and people's legs or ankles. Now, these behaviors can also occur in neutered dogs and can stem from over-excitement, lack of exercise, attempts to show dominance, or the dog simply not being taught that these behaviors are unacceptable. But neutering helps, too. Neutering keeps your dog from chasing females in heat. A female in heat gives off chemicals that can be scented from a mile away. An intact male can become very agitated – whining, pacing, sometimes escaping his house or yard. Neutering puts an end to all that. Neutering reduces the risk of prostate disorders. Enlarged prostate occurs in 80% of intact male dogs past the age of five. Affected dogs have difficulty with urination or bowel movements. The good news is that it's fixable. If you neuter at that time, the prostate will shrink quickly and the problems will resolve. Prostate cysts and prostate infections, though, can be harder to treat. Neutering prevents testicular cancer. About 7% of intact males develop a testicular tumor. It seldom spreads and has a cure rate over 90%, but neutering prevents it entirely. If your dog is a year old and still has one or both testicles tucked up inside his body (called cryptorchidism), the retained testicle is 14 times as likely to develop a tumor compared to a descended testicle. A cryptorchid dog should definitely be neutered. Neutering reduces the risk of perianal fistula. This is a painful skin disease where infected boils develop around a dog's anus. It is extremely difficult to treat. It can appear in any dog, but is most common in non-neutered German Shepherds, Irish Setters, and Leonbergers. Neutering prevents your dog from breeding. The dog population in the United States is out of control. Every day dogs are put to sleep because there are not enough homes for them. If you breed your male dog, his puppies would take homes away from the poor dogs who are already here. What if your male dog passed along genes for a health problem? A dog who is allowed to breed must first be tested and cleared of certain health problems known to be hereditary. Imagine a puppy living with a painful health problem because your male dog had that problem in his genes yet was allowed to breed. You would feel sad and guilty. It's a big responsibility to own an intact male dog. You must be extra careful to keep him away from unspayed females. Neutering Your Male Dog – Pros and Cons (You might want to look at the cons, too.)

Question: I’m looking to buy a Rottweiler what are hip and elbow scores?
Answer: What do hip and elbow scores mean? HIP SCORE: A hip score is a measure of evidence of hip dysplasia (abnormal development). Scores for each hip are added together to get an overall hip score for a dog. Scores range from 0 to 106, with the lower the score the better. The advice to breeders is to ideally breed only from dogs which score below the breed average. Breed average for Rottweiler is 13 (Breed Average Hip Scores - Vetrica) Hip Dysplasia Hip dysplasia is the most common inherited orthopaedic disease in large and giant breed dogs, and occurs in many medium-sized breeds as well. The hip joint is a “ball and socket” joint; the “ball” (the top part of the thigh bone or femur) fits into a “socket” (acetabulum) formed by the pelvis. If there is a loose fit between these bones, and the ligaments which help to hold them together are loose, the ball may slide part way out of the socket (subluxate). The mode of inheritance is polygenic (caused by many different genes). Scientists do not yet know which genes are involved, or how many genes. Factors that can make the disease worse includes excess weight, a fast growth rate, and high-calorie or supplemented diets. X-rays are taken when the dog is over one year old, then the x-rays are sent to the BVA for scoring. The hip-scoring system warrants explanation as it is quite confusing for the uninitiated. The score is determined by allocating points to each imperfection on the ball and socket of each hip joint. The minimum (best) score for each hip is 0, while the maximum (worst) is 53, making a total of 106 when multiplied by two for both hips. Basically: the higher the score, the more likelihood of Hip Dysplasia developing. The hip scores should be well within the average (mean) score for the breed, which, currently, is 13 for the Rottweiler. The BVA advise that breeders wishing to try to control HD should breed only from animals with hip scores below the breed mean score. So, if the parents of your puppy have scores below 13, then that would be an indication that your puppy should have sound hips. If the parents had a score of 0:0 then that would be perfect scores! You should look for scores as even as possible e.g. you don’t want an uneven number such as 1:12, as this could indicate a problem in one hip. If possible, try to ascertain the scores of the ancestors of the puppy’s parents. Some breeders note these on the animal’s pedigree. The recommendation is to breed from the lowest hip scores, the Rottweiler Club Code of Ethics for members states that the highest score which can be bred from is 16, with no more than 8 on either hip.i.e. 8/8. The lower the score the better. The disease is progressive. (Health) ELBOW SCORE: Rottweilers had a mean total elbow score of 1.04 compared with 0.51 in Labrador retrievers. Rottweiler males had a significantly higher ED score than females (p = 0.005), but in Labrador retrievers this was not the case (p = 0.603) although males did have higher scores than females. Question: Do dogs get sad when their puppies are taken away?
Answer: Your question about whether or not dogs “get sad when their puppies are taken away” interests me. If we think about it, the answer must be “Timing is everything.” If the pups are taken away too soon, the “Do dogs get sad answer” is yes. A very sad truth is that too many times puppies are taken away from their mother and their litter-mates too soon: 8 weeks is the legal minimum PUPPIES LEAVING THEIR MOM IS — & SHOULD BE — A NATURAL PROCESS: “When it’s time for a mother dog to wean her puppies, she knows what to do naturally. “Generally, a mother dog begins to wean her puppies at about three or four weeks of age. Weaning usually ends at about eight weeks, but it is a gradual process over a period of weeks, not an instant removal of nursing. “During the nursing period, the puppies are beginning to learn proper behavior and socialization skills from their mother and through the interactions with their siblings. They also get nurturing and bonding during the nursing period, so they have a sense of belonging. Because a puppy’s vision is limited in the first couple weeks, they need to stay close to their mother. Nursing is not only food and nutrition; it provides a sense of security for the puppies. “Teething begins at about three or four weeks. Those razor sharp little puppy teeth, sometimes referred to as milk teeth, can hurt their mother when a puppy is nursing. The irritation can be something that inspires the mother dog to begin to wean as the pain of those sharp teeth increases. If you’ve ever been nipped by a puppy and felt how painful those sharp teeth can be, you have an inkling of what the mother is feeling when she nurses. “The mother may decide to cut off nursing altogether on her own. She may push the puppies away and refuse to nurse.” How to Help a Mother Dog Wean Her Puppies SO, AT THE APPROPRIATE TIME, MOM IS HAPPY TO SEE HER PUPPIES GO TO A NEW HOME.

For us, a pup is a lifetime commitment: We insist on a happy, healthy, well-adjusted pup who comes from folks who take care to properly socialize the puppies. We go to see the litter, meet the mama-dog, and see for ourselves where our pup would come from. We insist on vet records and appropriate guarantees from the breeder. We immediately take our pup to our vet and have our pup thoroughly vet-checked. The breeder is all-important. The perfect pup is all-important. For us the breed standards and the breeder are most important when finding our perfect pup. We use the internet, looking at various breeders to see what each was offering — and rejecting breeder after breeder, until we found a promising few. With Trixie, we had located her breeder via the internet, liked the look of the puppies and the full-grown mastiff parents, had spoken with the breeder via telephone and liked what she had to say, so we drove 400 miles (round-trip, Baton Rouge, LA, to Dallas, TX) to visit the breeder in person and inspect her pups. Question: How do you feel about trainers using shock collars for dog obedience?
Answer: There is absolutely no reason to use a shock collar: Shock collars are “overkill.” If a trainer does not have the ability to establish a working relationship with a dog, then he or she needs to reconsider being a trainer. What you want is for the puppy to want to obey you, not because of fear, but because of trust, love and joy. Think about it: First-class field trainers (and hunters, etc.) use a whistle (using whistles for field training) to communicate with their dogs. In field trials work or in hunting, the dog responds to a whistle, not a shock. Praise and accomplishment and a job well done are the dog and his/her trainer’s reward. A whistle is an extension of the dog-trainer’s voice. Voice training means that the trainer has total control over his own voice (or whistle): With voice-control, there are never any “accidental shocks.” The trainer’s voice is always at hand to use with the dog. So, skip the shock-collar and skip the treats: Train with something your dog can hear and rely on, knowing that his/her response will bring praise for a job well done. I strongly suggest that you train your pup/dog yourself: You and your pup/dog may choose to work with and be guided by a trainer, but you need to know what “dog training” should be.
